I

JOHN R. HEISNER

Grand Master – 2016-2017
Most Worshipful Brother John Richard Heisner was raised a Master
Mason in Eugene Lodge No. 11 under the jurisdiction of the Grand
Lodge of Oregon on March 5, 1969. He affiliated with Amity Lodge No.
442 in San Diego in 1985. He served as master of that lodge in 2004, and
in 2013, he was recognized with the Hiram Award.
Brother Heisner’s service to the Grand Lodge began that same year.
He served two terms on the Research Committee and two terms on the
Jurisprudence Committee. He served as inspector of the 909th Masonic
District for five years, completed a three-year term as a trustee of the
Masonic Homes of California, and is a founding member of the Public
Schools Advisory Council in San Diego. In 2012, Brother Heisner served
as grand orator for Most Worshipful Brother Frank Loui, calling upon
his strong knowledge of Masonic symbolism; he is the author of four
books on this subject.
Brother Heisner is a 33° Inspector General Honorary of the San
Diego Scottish Rite Bodies and a member of Al Bahr Shrine. He is also
a member of the San Diego York Rite Bodies, the San Diego Conclave of
the Red Cross of Constantine, the Rosicrucian College, and the Southern
California Past Masters Association. He is one of the founding members
of Lux Lodge No. 846, a California traditional observance Masonic lodge.
In 2014, he was invested with the DeMolay Honorary Legion of Honor.
In 2015, he was inducted as a fellow of the Philalethes Society.
Brother Heisner is a partner at Heisner Alvarez, APC, a business
litigation and trusts and estates law firm in La Jolla. He has conducted
more than 100 jury trials, first as a government prosecutor and then as
a private practitioner.

JOHN R. HEISNER

Grand Master
October 30, 2016 - October 15, 2017

Brother Heisner is active in his community, formerly serving as a
trustee for the San Diego Maritime Museum and member of the board
of trustees of the San Diego Chapter of the St. Jude Hospital Foundation.
He is a member of St. Luke’s and All Hallows churches in San Diego and
La Jolla. Additionally, Brother Heisner served as an adjunct professor
for the University of San Diego School of Law for 14 years, teaching
trial advocacy.
Brother Heisner lives in La Jolla with his wife, Margo. He has four
adult children and 10 grandchildren.

I, ALLAN L. CASALOU, Grand Secretary of the M\W\ Grand Lodge
of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California, do hereby
certify that the following pages contain a true and faithful transcript
of the proceedings of that body at its One Hundred Sixty-eighth
Annual Communication, commencing at the City of San Francisco,
Friday the Thirteenth of October, A.L. 6017 and terminating on
Sunday the Fifteenth of October, A.L. 6017.

I have hereunto appended my official signature and have affixed
the seal of the M\W\ Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of the State of California, at the office of the Grand Secretary, this
First day of January, in the year of Light, two thousand and eighteen.

Grand Secretary

3

One Hundred Sixty-Eighth
Annual Communication
Friday Afternoon, October 13, 2017
The 168th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Free and
Accepted Masons of the State of California was called to order by Grand
Master John R. Heisner on Friday, October 13, 2017.
Worshipful Brother James B. McCord, Master of Lux Lodge No. 846,
raised the opening session of Grand Lodge. The gavel used to raise
Grand Lodge was Grand Master Heisner’s father’s gavel from his time
as Master of Mineral King Lodge No. 128 (Dinuba No. 385). The gavel
dates back to at least 1951.
Reception of the Past Grand Masters
The Grand Master welcomed the brethren and directed the Grand
Marshal to present the Past Grand Masters of the Grand Lodge of
California at the Altar. The Grand Marshal then introduced each Past
Grand Master, then the Grand Master and Deputy Grand Master
personally greeted each one. The Grand Master asked the brethren to
join him in saluting our Past Grand Masters by the battery of three times
three. The Past Grand Masters were then escorted to seats reserved for
them in the auditorium. The Grand Master then directed the Grand
Secretary to send to each absent Past Grand Master the usual letter of
greeting from the Grand Lodge.
Roll Call
The Grand Secretary was asked to call the roll of Grand Lodge
Officers, Past Grand Masters, and Past Grand Officers, and to ascertain
if a constitutional number were present to convene the Grand Lodge of
California. The following were present as indicated by their response to
the calling of the roll:

Report, there were 829 Master Masons registered as of 12 p.m. Friday,

The Grand Master then opened Grand Lodge in ancient form. The
Grand Marshal and the Deacons retired to escort the flag of the United

Keynote Address

Saturday Morning, October 14, 2017

Ronald A. Seale
This year marks the Tercentenary Anniversary of the United Grand
Lodge of England. Ronald A. Seale, 33°, Sovereign Grand Commander,
Supreme Council Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite of Freemasonry,
Southern Jurisdiction, U.S.A delivered a keynote speech highlighting
this auspicious occasion.
At 5:02 p.m. the Grand Master called Grand Lodge from labor to
refreshment, to be called on again at 8:30 a.m. on Saturday, October 14.

11

Chaplain, the Grand Master noted that Grand Lodge was raised by
Worshipful Brother Derrick L. Howard, Master of Amity Lodge No. 442.
Brother Howard raised Grand Lodge using a gavel and sounding block he
had presented to the Grand Master at the York Rite Four Way Reception
in Van Nuys.

The Grand Master then directed the Grand Marshal to escort the

asked the brethren to join him in saluting our District Inspectors by the
battery of three times three.

Video Presentation from the
California Masonic Foundation Board of Trustees
The Grand Master directed attention to the video screen for the Report
of the California Masonic Foundation Board of Trustees (Appendix J).
At 11:14 a.m., the Grand Master asked the brethren to pause in the
deliberations for the annual Memorial Service.

The Grand Master called on the Very Reverend John O. McQuown,
Grand Chaplain, to present a service of remembrance for our departed
brethren. His remarks were as follows:
We take pause this afternoon to remember those Brothers who have
this year ended their earthly toils and entered the Celestial Lodge above
where the doors are never closed nor eyes dimmed with sorrow. These
Brothers and friends have laid down their working tools and, though no
longer with us physically, are still in our hearts and thoughts. They have
been examples to us as teachers, mentors, and family members. Their
good works, assistance, and kind acts will always be remembered and
serve as guides to our own conduct. In this way, they are still among us.
Take this moment to reflect on at least one Brother whom you admired
and who had a positive effect on your life. Remember how he lived and
contributed to us, his family, his Lodge, this Fraternity, and his country.
We should all strive to make our lives as good and admirable as his. This
is as close to immortality as any of us can hope for.
With sad hearts we say to these Brothers:
“Soft and safe to thee, my brethren, be thy resting place! Bright and
glorious be thy rising from it! Fragrant be the acacia sprig that there
shall flourish! May the earliest buds of spring unfold their beauties
o’er thy resting place, and there may the sweetness of the summer’s
last rose linger longest! Though the winds of autumn may destroy the
loveliness of their existence, yet the destruction is not final, and in the
springtime, they shall surely bloom again. So, in the bright morning
of the resurrection, thy spirit shall spring into the newness of life and
expand in immortal beauty, in realms beyond the skies. Until then, our
dear Brothers, until then; farewell.”
Amen.

At 11:15 a.m. the Grand Master called Grand Lodge from labor to
refreshment, to be called again at 1:15 p.m. sharp.

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Election of Officers

Election of Junior Grand Warden

The Grand Master then explained the balloting procedure for the
election of officers. No ballot would be necessary if the office was not
contested. If more than one nomination was received for an office, the
white ballot card would be used.

The Grand Master announced that pursuant to Section 404.420 of
the California Masonic Code, Worshipful Brother Arthur H. Weiss, a
Past Master of Conejo Valley Lodge No. 807 in Thousand Oaks, had
been recommended for the office of Junior Grand Warden of the Grand
Lodge of California for the ensuing Grand Lodge Year. The Grand Orator
then read the biography previously circulated in accordance with this
section, while Brother Weiss stood before Grand Lodge. He was then
escorted to the Grand Tiler’s Room, while other nominations were
called for. None appearing, Right Worshipful Brother John E. Trauner,
Junior Grand Warden, moved that the Grand Secretary be instructed
to cast a unanimous ballot for Worshipful Arthur H. Weiss to serve as
Junior Grand Warden for the ensuing Grand Lodge Year. The motion
was seconded by the Grand Lecturer and unanimously carried. Upon
his return to the floor of the Grand Lodge and upon his acceptance, he
was declared unanimously elected by the Grand Master.

Election of the Grand Master
Deputy Grand Master Bruce R. Galloway was nominated Grand
Master by Most Worshipful Brother Frank Loui, Past Grand Master.
No further nominations appearing, it was moved by Most Worshipful
Brother Frank Loui, seconded and carried that the nominations be
closed, and that the Grand Secretary be instructed to cast a unanimous
ballot for Right Worshipful Bruce R. Galloway to serve as Grand Master
for the ensuing Grand Lodge year. Upon his acceptance, he was declared
unanimously elected.
Election of Deputy Grand Master
Senior Grand Warden Stuart A. Wright was nominated Deputy Grand
Master by Most Worshipful Brother Frederick L. Sorsabal, Past Grand
Master. No further nominations appearing, it was moved, seconded, and
carried that the nominations be closed, and that the Grand Secretary
be instructed to cast a unanimous ballot for Right Worshipful Stuart A.
Wright to serve as Deputy Grand Master for the ensuing Grand Lodge
year. Upon his acceptance, he was declared unanimously elected.
Election of Senior Grand Warden
Junior Grand Warden John E. Trauner was nominated Senior Grand
Warden by Most Worshipful Brother Russell E. Charvonia, Past Grand
Master. No further nominations appearing, it was moved, seconded, and
carried that the nominations be closed, and that the Grand Secretary
be instructed to cast a unanimous ballot for Right Worshipful John E.
Trauner to serve as Senior Grand Warden for the ensuing Grand Lodge
year. Upon his acceptance, he was declared unanimously elected.

and Grand Lecturer

Presentation of the Joe Jackson Award
The Masonic Homes of California and our Grand Lodge were pleased
to present an award in memory of our late Brother Joe Jackson.
Joe Jackson, a Mason for 60 years and Hiram Award recipient, served
Joseph L. Shell Daylight Lodge No. 837 and Heartland Lodge No. 576
for 17 years as Secretary, Assistant Secretary, Ttreasurer, and Chaplain.
Joe exemplified Masonic Relief and Brotherly Love. He reached out
to members and widows on a weekly basis; assisted with numerous
applications to MOS and the Masonic Homes; frequently called Masonic
Assistance to check the status of his member’s applications; and helped
expedite the paperwork process. Joe was a catalyst for launching the
successful Lodge Outreach Program in Division IX. Joe passed away
in 2012, leaving a legacy that set a worthy example for extending
Masonic relief.

Miss Sarah Colbert
Miss California Job’s Daughters
Good Morning Most Worshipful John Heisner, Grand Master of Masons
in California, Worshipful Masters, Master Masons, and distinguished
guests. My name is Sarah Colbert and I am Miss California Job’s
Daughter for 2017-2018.
I would like to congratulate all the Grand Lodge Officers on a successful
year during this very special 300th anniversary of Freemasonry. I would
also like to extend my best wishes to the incoming Grand Lodge Officers.
I would like to take this time to share some history of Job’s Daughters
with you. Job’s Daughters was founded in 1920 by Mrs. Ethel T. Wead
Mick in Omaha, Nebraska. The Order was created for the purpose of
developing leadership skills, public speaking skills, character, and
lifelong friendships in young women between the ages of 10 and 20.
Here is a glimpse into my Job’s Daughters story. When I became a Job’s
Daughter, I was 10 years old. But, I was a really shy 10 year old. I was the
little girl who would sink down in my seat when the teacher was calling
on people. Speaking in front of the class was my biggest fear and I was
scared to death of people talking to me.
The first office I was appointed to in the Bethel was 4th Messenger.
The duty of the 4th Messenger is to explain to the Initiates the 4th part
of the Story of Job during the Ceremony of Initiation. This requires a

Although I strongly disliked the station of 4th messenger as a 10 year
old, this experience sparked a passion for ritual work in me. Following
this station, I went on to accept more responsibilities in the Bethel,
learning and performing more of the Job’s Daughters ritual. I soon
went on to learn all five parts of the Story of Job and have competed
in the Story of Job Ritual Competition for the last five years at our
Grand Bethel.
Now look where I am today, precisely the last place my 10-year-old self
would have wanted to be. I didn’t realize it during this time, but these
ritual competitions were teaching me very important public speaking
skills. To me, I was just participating in some competitions with my youth
order, but along the way I was developing confidence, leadership skills,
public speaking skills, and poise, all while I was doing what I enjoyed.
This is exactly what our founder envisioned for our members.
I progressed through the line of elected officers in Bethel No. 289,
Granada Hills and became a Past Honored Queen. Along the way,
I was given more responsibilities with planning events, organizing
fundraisers and presiding over ritualistic ceremonies. I held the office
of Honored Queen from June to December in 2014 where I planned our
whole installation ceremony, a calendar of meetings, fundraisers and
fun events for the Bethel, along with a balanced budget.
In 2017, I competed for the title of Miss California Job’s Daughter.
This competition includes a written test on the laws and rules of Job’s
Daughters International, a ritual recitation, an interview and a final
question on stage at our Grand Bethel Session. All things that my
10-year-old self would have been terrified of.
The point of this story is that Job’s Daughters has taught me so much
and strengthened my confidence. All these things have helped me in all
aspects of life and given me the courage to set high goals for myself for
the future. I can’t even imagine the type of person I would have been
had I never become involved in our beautiful order.

I firmly believe that Job’s Daughters is teaching the women of the
future how to be strong; but not just strong, Jobie Strong. It is not just
the strength to obey, but the strength to lead. It is not just the strength
in numbers, but the strength of sisters. Not just the strength to lift,
but the strength to raise. And not just the strength to get yourself over,
but the strength to get over yourself. There’s strong, and then there’s
Jobie Strong.

Lexi Harris, Northern California DeMolay’s Sweetheart, and Shawn

It’s been eight years since I took my first steps on my journey into
this Masonic community, this Masonic family. Eight years since I joined
DeMolay and began to find the benefits of the support found within this
community. I have gotten more out of this journey than I ever would
have thought possible.
I was the first of my siblings to take a step into this world, but since
then they have all followed suit. My littlest sister is on track to lead
our local Bethel, my younger brother is a Past Master Councilor of our
chapter, and my closest sister was a Grand Officer just this last year.
Because of these shared threads I have been able to enjoy a closer
relationship with my siblings than many of my peers. It’s been nearly
a decade of my life spent within this circle, and I know my family isn’t
the only one who has been so positively impacted by Masonry; many
others are closer today than they would have been without the Masonic
family. Though it may not often be said, I believe that it’s the community
surrounding Masons, and the qualities it encourages that brings out the
best in people.
DeMolay has given me many great gifts, but none more valuable
than the opportunity to enter into this community that is so dedicated
to making good men better. There’s more to be found than affirmation

The Masons of California have every right to be proud of the Masonic
family you have nurtured in recent years, and for how that has impacted
the youth orders of California. Masons build the foundation of all of
the youth groups, and they form the backbone of the adult leadership
within. Every Mason can have the potential to use their experience to
aid the Youth Orders to find greater success. From the very beginning,
Masonry has made the Youth Orders possible and, by extension, has
ensured their success.
It is your support that has made the growth and success of the youth
orders possible. I thank you all for what you have done in the past and
what you will continue to do to encourage the development of the young
men of DeMolay so that they may be the best men they can be and,
when the time comes, they can be the best Masons they can be.
In conclusion, I’d like to leave an open invitation to everyone to attend

Miss Alana Clement, Grand Worthy Advisor
International Order of Rainbow
Good afternoon Most Worshipful Grand Master; Officers and members
of Grand Lodge; Distinguished and honored guests; and friends of
California Rainbow. Thank you for allowing me to speak to you on
behalf of the International Order of the Rainbow for Girls in California.
My family has always been the outdoorsy type. My brother and I were
both involved in scouting and our parents were actively involved as
leaders of our troops. Each summer we would go on road trips across
California and see the landmarks that others rave about. Before bed,
we’d bond around a campfire while making some s’mores for dessert. In
the morning when we woke up, we were embraced by the crisp, summer
air and the condensation that had pooled up on the side of our tent.
We’d then take in the beauty of the outdoors.

30

31

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

One of the most beautiful aspects about Northern California has
always been our breathtaking giant Redwood Trees. Their tall, large
frames have stood their ground for thousands of years. Each year, trees
add another ring to their trunks. They give those who study them a
glimpse into their history. These trees have seen many seasons come
and go. Many animals have been supported by their protective branches.
They’ve even survived many natural disasters, and they still stand tall
and proud.

Just like the Redwoods that have been around for years, we can make
sure that we keep adding rings onto our trunk so that we can stand tall
and tell others that our Masonic Tree is here to stay. So stand tall, be
present and tell others your story. Thank you.

Our Masonic family reminds me of our California Redwoods. As
you celebrate 300 years of Freemasonry, our family has withstood the
test of time. For anything to last that long, means that it’s here to stay.
Our tree was once a sapling, but has since grown to be stronger than
ever before. Your trunk has been able to hold up and support many
branches of our family, such as Eastern Star, Job’s Daughters, DeMolay,
and even Rainbow. You have helped to keep our traditions, values and
teachings alive.
However, every now and then even the Giant Redwoods can come
crashing down and I hate to say it but even a tree as sturdy as ours
can fall. Every part of our tree is currently in a drought, we are being
neglected of the membership that we need in order to continue to grow.
But there are things we can all do in order to protect our tree to make
it sturdy once more.
This year, Rainbow has started a leadership program that focuses on
the roots of our individual tree: our youngest members. They are the
most important girls in our order, because they are the ones who will
be able to make sure that our Rainbow lessons can be taught for many
more years. We are teaching them to “Be Present.” The program focuses
on teaching our young girls to be an active part of today’s society. The
program already expands on our other lessons in Rainbow and helps
them to find their voice and step up to become the leaders of tomorrow.
Our whole Masonic Family has traditions and teachings that should
be preserved similar to the sap in a tree. If we want to continue to grow
we need to adapt to our environment so that we can all become a little
more relevant in today’s fast-paced society. Remind others of why we
joined our family. Show the world that we can’t be chopped down, not
without a fight.

Masonic Youth Leadership Scholarship Awards

Sunday, October 15, 2017
INSTALLATION OF GRAND LODGE OFFICERS

This year, the California Masonic Foundation created the Masonic
Youth Leadership Scholarship for the youth leaders of the four Masonic
Youth Orders in California. The Masonic Youth Leadership Scholarship
focuses on a particular segment of the talented, dedicated, and deserving
members of these Youth Orders – their state and regional leaders. These
leaders include the Rainbow Grand Assembly Officers; Job’s Daughters
Grand Bethel Officers; and the DeMolay jurisdiction, division, and
league officers. All Awardees present stood for recognition.
The Grand Master then gave his closing remarks and expressed his
honor and privilege at having been given the opportunity to serve the
Craft as Grand Master.

41

Grand Master’s Message
Members of the Grand Lodge – my brethren all,
Welcome to the 168th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge
of California, and please join me in extending a warm welcome to the
out-of-state visitors who are joining us during this memorable moment
in our Masonic history. Three hundred years ago, on June 24, 1717,
the first Masonic Grand Lodge was formed in London. This Annual
Communication, in addition to recognizing our achievements here in
California, honors the past of our great fraternity, and contemplates its
place – and our role as Masons – in the world today.
Throughout this fraternal year, we have joined our global brotherhood
in recognizing this milestone occasion. With the help of dedicated
Masons from Division VIII, we created a short commemorative video,
which was shared in communities throughout the state. In June, Margo
and I joined more than 170 brothers and friends on an extraordinary
journey to Ireland, Scotland, and England to celebrate the 300th
anniversary of Freemasonry in its birthplace and to visit the enduring
monuments of our fraternal past. It was the trip of a lifetime, and one
that we will treasure for many years to come. On the evening of June 24
– the feast day of Freemasonry’s patron saint, St. John the Baptist, and
exactly 300 years after the founding of the first Grand Lodge – many of
the Master Masons on our trip met our United Kingdom brethren at the
Carlton Club in London for an elaborate and memorable St. John’s Day
feast. Hosted by the Metropolitan Grand Lodge of London, it was a true
highlight of our journey, exceeding our most intimate expectations of
how an elegant Masonic dining experience might unfold.
Throughout our time abroad, our band of travelers bonded closely
with each other, and each of us was inspired and encouraged by our
journey. Many of us had never met before, but we soon became great
friends. We all enjoyed the privilege of experiencing warm fellowship
with our brethren in these countries as we spoke with them, and lived
beside them. I was reminded throughout our travels that something
special happens when we go beyond simply greeting each other in
passing: When we are willing to make an effort to truly understand each
other and to appreciate our unique experiences, we can gain insight
from each other’s perspectives, be welcomed alongside each other’s
families, and develop deep, meaningful connections.

42

43

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

This 300th anniversary has presented an excellent opportunity
for Masons and grand lodges around the world to establish stronger
connections. Perhaps the desire to reach outward comes easily to
our Grand Lodge, as California Masonry’s rich history began during
the difficult times of the Gold Rush. Our forefathers quickly learned
the importance of giving of themselves, and, equally valuable, of
building relationships with others who could be depended upon in
kind. This pioneer spirit – an appreciation for both independence and
interdependence – has become ingrained in the souls of California
Masons as one of our greatest lessons.

We continue to support our Masonic connections in further parts of
the world as well. In addition to meeting with brothers in the United
Kingdom, we attended the Annual Communications of the National
Grand Lodge of France and the Grand Lodge of the Philippines this year.
There, we met fellow Masonic leaders, renewed friendships, developed
new bonds and strengthened our worldwide fraternal connections.
I have enjoyed my association with all these grand lodges and their
leaders over the years. As this fraternal year comes to an end, I am
confident that our bonds are stronger than ever and that Freemasonry in
California is well served by our continued association and brotherhood.

Our open-minded perspective has allowed us to nurture strong ties
with the grand lodges that surround us. We greatly value our close bonds
with the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California, Inc. and the Grand
Lodge of Iran in Exile, with whom we share this jurisdiction. We lay
cornerstones together, march in parades together, attend conferences
together, and share meals together. Most importantly, we listen to one
another and consider each other’s perspectives as we make plans to
move our brotherhood forward. This spring, we gathered together in
Pasadena for a cornerstone ceremony at the new Shriner’s Hospital
for Children. Each Grand Master was introduced and met with loud
applause. Dr. Donald Ware, Grand Master of Prince Hall Masons in
California, delivered an inspiring oration. It was a powerful moment
of unity for all those in attendance. Each summer for nearly 40 years,
we have participated in the Conference of Three Californias, meeting
with our fellow California Grand Lodges – Baja California and Baja
California Sur. This gathering remains an important opportunity for us
to unite and share ideas across borders. The Grand Lodge of Iran in
Exile and the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California joined us for this
year’s conference in Baja. We were heartened that the Grand Lodge of
Baja Sur formally extended recognition to the Grand Lodge of Iran in
Exile during the meeting.

Sometimes we must look outside our Grand Lodge to truly appreciate
what we have, and my travels beyond our jurisdiction leave no doubt
in my mind about the Grand Lodge of California’s importance and
leadership in the Masonic world. We continue to be one of the world’s
most resourceful, well-organized, and progressive grand lodges.
This knowledge is a reminder to us all that in addition to striving for
excellence for our own members, we must continue to innovate and
collaborate with those who turn to us for inspiration and guidance.

We are active in the Western Conference of Grand Lodges, which
includes Masonic leaders from Alaska, Arizona, British Columbia,
Hawaii, Oregon and Washington. I am pleased to report that at the
most recent meeting of the conference this past February, the Prince
Hall Grand Lodge of California, Inc. was unanimously elected to full
membership. This was an important step forward in breaking down
barriers to unity and promoting harmonious relationships.

It is with this perspective that I approach my message to you today.
While my complete report will be available in the official Proceedings of
this Annual Communication, I would like to take this time to share with
you my observations about the current general condition of California
Freemasonry. Several milestone moments this year have captured the
essence of who we are, what we are doing and where we are headed as
a fraternity.
There is a growing interest among California Masons in combining
ritual experiences with opportunities for Masonic fellowship. During
these occasions, lasting friendships are formed over fabulous dining and
conversation. The MGM (Manlalakbay Na Gurong Mason or Traveling
Master Masons group) met twice this year: once at a festive board that I
attended, and once at Crocker Lodge for a degree-team ritual conferral.
In July, I attended a “Masonathon” hosted by Division IX lodges in San
Diego – a daylong Masonic ritual feast where specially selected ritualists
conferred the three degrees of Masonry upon candidates. These
and other examples indicate a welcome trend of how our members
are seeking to create thoughtful and unique Masonic experiences.
Underscoring Masonry’s thirst for knowledge, we once again held two
significant events to highlight Masonic studies and share important

44

45

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

scholarship. The Fifth International Conference on Freemasonry at
UCLA gave new insights into how Freemasonry’s past continues to
have an impact upon member experiences today. It was followed a few
months later by the California Masonic Symposium, which focused on
the pillage of Masonic archives during World War II. These important
gatherings connected many historical dots about the fraternity’s role in
advancing human rights around the world, and helped us understand
that deep knowledge of Masonry’s values goes hand-in-glove with our
sacred ritual. Together, they can have formidable power, capable of
transforming the way people think and behave.

heritage. Most Worshipful Warren is, without a doubt, one of the most
influential figures of the 20th century. Our Grand Lodge is planning to
appropriately honor his legacy. A committee has been formed to explore
ways to do so, and it is hoped that plans for this important project will
come to fruition in the next year.

With this in mind, our Inspectors are working to deepen members’
connections to the ritual and to help them truly understand how
reflecting upon its lessons can amplify the significance of Masonry in
their lives. Many of our lodge Masters and Wardens are also encouraging
members to deeply examine who they are as individuals and what
their purpose is in life. This resurgence in Masonic leadership is a very
welcome trend, and it compels us to recall the California Masons of
the past who have been among the finest examples of humanity – men
who contributed massively to our fraternity, our state, our country and
the world.
Among these good men are more than 20 brethren who became eligible
to receive the Diamond Jubilee Award during my tenure as Grand Master.
This special designation recognizes Master Masons who have remained
members in good standing for 75 years. Each presentation gave us a
special opportunity to reflect upon the recipients’ Masonic journey and
the brothers they have touched and mentored throughout their lives. As
we consider our forefathers, we cannot help but remember Brother Earl
Warren. During the 20th century, perhaps none set a worthier example
than he. Warren’s illustrious career included service as a United States
Supreme Court chief justice, United States attorney general, Governor
of California, and Grand Master of our Most Worshipful Grand Lodge.
Each of these accomplishments was an achievement in its own right.
Viewed together, they represent a stirring tribute to how a good
brother persevered to share his Masonic light with the world. Among
his accomplishments are the Supreme Court’s landmark decisions he
presided over in Brown v. Board of Education, which eliminated racial
segregation in public schools; and Loving v. Virginia, which overturned
state laws banning interracial marriages. Many of his writings on these
transformational cases were deeply rooted in his Masonic values and

Of course, the insight we gain from studying our past is best applied
towards planning for our Masonic future. The Executive Committee
remains committed to consistently evaluating the leadership within our
jurisdiction to best support our statewide membership. During the latter
part of 2016, we reduced the number of Masonic Divisions from 10 to
nine. Each division now includes approximately the same number of
lodges, making oversight more balanced and cohesive. We will continue
to monitor this structure and will make adjustments, if needed. We are
lucky to have highly capable men leading our Fraternity in its current
state, and I remain proud of our jurisdiction’s track record of cultivating
strong Masonic leaders. I have greatly benefitted from the high-caliber
men who have stood beside me throughout my term as grand master,
and I look forward to seeing many new good men step into leadership
roles within our Craft.
Our future, of course, always rests in the hands of the next generation,
and I am grateful to the Youth Orders Committee, led by Most Worshipful
Larry Adamson, for continually encouraging creative collaboration
among the adult leadership. Last year, Most Worshipful M. David Perry
introduced new Masonic Youth Leadership Scholarships, which assist
eligible and dedicated leaders of DeMolay, Job’s Daughters and Rainbow
for Girls in obtaining a higher education. These scholarships continue
this year and are likely to endure in the years to come. We also continued
to support the Lx Week youth leadership experience workshops as part
of our dedication to strengthening Masonic Youth leaders.
We are engaged in inspiring growth within our fraternity as well.
Since 2016, this Grand Lodge has instituted more than a dozen new
lodges that are currently working under dispensation. Green Dragon
Masonic Fellowship Lodge No. 857 was granted its charter at the 2016
Annual Communication, and many of the lodges currently working
under dispensation will likely receive your approval to be constituted
during this Annual Communication. Our new lodge growth is closely
tied to our belief that Freemasonry works best when we become
builders, empowering our members to create the brotherhood and
lodge experiences that they are seeking.

46

47

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Through the process of actively nurturing new Masonic lodges, we
have gained a better understanding of lodge lifecycles. Lodges are living
organizations with fluid identities that are affected by new members and
those who move on. Lodges that are able to cooperatively pull together
and evolve when times change are more likely to endure than lodges
that are greatly burdened by unfamiliar situations and ambiguity. When
left unchecked, negative practices and mindsets can destroy a lodge.

Throughout this past Masonic year, it has been my privilege and
honor to serve as your Grand Master. I thoroughly enjoyed my time as
the temporary custodian of the Grand Oriental Chair, but you may rest
assured that our jurisdiction’s future leadership is in steady hands. I
know Bruce, Stu, and John; they are team builders and Masons of high
integrity who are intent on raising the future of this fraternity upon the
solid foundation of its past.

This term I was unfortunately compelled to suspend the charters
of three lodges – Pomona Lodge No. 246, East San Diego Lodge No.
561, and Napa Valley Lodge No. 93. Later, we will be considering the
revocation of Pomona’s charter and more time is needed at East San
Diego; however, I am happy to report that Napa Valley Lodge’s charter
was restored in August. In these matters, we must remain focused on
unity and our shared commitment to improving our fraternity and the
world around us.

Upon my installation as your Grand Master, I reminded you that the
freedoms born in the laboratories of Masonic lodges are Freemasonry’s
greatest gift: the freedom to say anything that doesn’t harm others; the
freedom to embrace any religion; freedom from fear, including fears of
poverty, indignity, hate and intolerance; and the freedom to seek and
pursue the knowledge required to retain these treasured liberties. It is
up to each of us to propagate this legacy, holding these freedoms as our
highest aims.

Masons are more visible today than ever before and a buzz of
excitement stirs whenever we appear in public. As we continue to
implement the 2020 Fraternity Plan, a growing number of lodges are
becoming powerful partners with their communities, effecting positive
change and raising the public profile of our fraternity. It was my
privilege as Grand Master to lay cornerstones at six public ceremonies.
We marched in parades and spoke with people in every community
we visited.

As you continue to build your personal Masonic legacy – during this
Annual Communication, amongst the brethren in your lodge, at home
with your family and within the solace of your own heart – I urge you to
consider what it means for you to be truly free. You will likely find that
this is not a question that can be easily answered; that is the point. True
freedom is limitless. Like Masonry, it requires an ongoing quest. Our
desire to obtain freedom is twinned with that of smoothing our rough
ashlar: Only through dedication, scholarship, perseverance, love and
deep devotion of purpose will we discover life’s greatest aims.

We continue to enhance our public image by exhibiting our exceptional
philanthropic culture. Through the California Masonic Foundation, the
Fraternity’s chief fundraising arm, we are building literate children,
supporting public schools and relieving the distress of our brethren and
widows in need who rightfully depend upon us.
Some people say that Freemasonry is humanity’s conscience. Some
believe that Masonry is transformative, possessing the power to change
people’s perspectives. Others see Masonry as a force that advances
civilization. As California Masons, we know that all these lofty ideals are
grounded in truth. This year’s examination of Masonry’s past 300 years
– especially that history within California – has opened new doors of
inspiration. Behind them, we will discover new ideas with the capacity
to transform our personal Masonic experiences and to lead our Grand
Lodge towards new possibilities. Our receptiveness to new perspectives
and innovative ideas will surely become a part of the foundation upon
which we will continue to build our future.

Thank you for standing beside me on this pathway of my Masonic
journey. I look forward to seeing how each of you will charter the
directions to come.

Report of the Deputy Grand Master
2017-18 Grand Lodge Budget
Bruce R. Galloway, Deputy Grand Master
Brethren of the Grand Lodge of California,
I am pleased to present the following budget for the 2017-18 Grand
Lodge year. The budget sets forth in a summary and in detail, the
income and expenses anticipated for the next fiscal year.
What might be less apparent in the budget are all of the programs
and services that this budget makes possible. Our 2020 Fraternity
Plan identifies four key priorities: a rewarding member experience,
meaningful and memorable degrees, strong lodges and halls, and
our impact on society. This budget is focused on these priorities and
includes funding for the following programs and services:
• Masonic education, including support for events like
the International Conference on Freemasonry at UCLA,
the California Masonic Symposium, and the Candidate
Learning Center.
• Ritual education and training including ritual conferences for
inspectors, officers coaches and lodge officers and the annual
Ritual Competition
• Leadership training events including the Master and Wardens
Retreats, Secretary and Treasurer Retreats, Inspectors
Retreats, the Inspector Development Academy, and the Lodge
Management Certification Program.
• New lodge development efforts that have already resulted in
the creation of 14 new lodges throughout the state.
• Communications to Masons, widows, and the general public
including the lodge app, new lodge website templates, the
bimonthly publication of California Freemason magazine,
the monthly electronic newsletter The Leader sent to all
lodge officers, the weekly all-member email, as well as
the maintenance of seven websites and all of the social
media outlets.

68

Proceedings of the

• Community outreach that includes Grand Lodge events at
community libraries, courthouses, fire stations, and schools
throughout the state.
• Technology and data including iMember, the Member Center,
and the Vault.
• Information and service requests.
• Financial services to lodges and halls including accounting
services, tax return services, and tax-exempt status restoration.
• Real estate services and support including support and
consultation for building improvements, leases, sales,
and purchases.
This budget is based upon the per capita proposal approved at the last
Annual Communication by the Masters and Wardens of our Constituent
Lodges along with the other members of Grand Lodge. Since that time,
I have worked with the finance staff, the Grand Secretary, the Grand
Treasurer, and the Finance Committee to refine the budget based
on current information and membership data. I presented a draft of
this budget to the Masters and Wardens at the leadership retreats this
spring. Their input has been helpful in finalizing this work.
While the total membership ended up about 350 members lower than
we anticipated, we have managed to present a balanced budget for the
next fiscal year and preserve all of the programs and services that are
essential to the 2020 Plan.
Expenses exclusive of depreciation for the next fiscal year are
estimated to be $3,199,237. These expenses are divided between
fraternal, appropriations, programs, and general and administrative
expenses. The projected net revenue after expenses is $12,602. If
elected Grand Master, I will monitor the budget very closely each month
and seek the assistance of the Executive Committee, Grand Treasurer,
Grand Secretary, and the Finance Committee to see that we operate
according to it.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

69

As Deputy Grand Master, I remain confident about the future of our
Fraternity. Our past provides us with a strong foundation. Together, we
will honor our past while we shape our future so that future generations
will regard Freemasonry as a relevant and respected Fraternity worthy
of their time and consideration.
I appreciate your past support on the Per Capita proposal I made as
Senior Grand Warden, and I thank you for your support now as we lay
the groundwork for positive and productive year in 2018!

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Proceedings of the

Fiscal Year 2017-18
Bruce R. Galloway, Deputy Grand Master
Revenue Analysis

The Grand Lodge has several sources of income. Historically, the primary revenue sources have been Per
Capita and degree fees. The Grand Lodge Endowment Fund was created in 1992 and generates income from
the investment return. To better manage the income from the Endowment, a 4.5 percent spending policy has
been instituted, calculated on a rolling five-year average valuation to protect the fund principle. The Grand
Lodge may from time to time have other income, such as interest from bank accounts and other financial
instruments. In 2004, the California Masonic Foundation included in its mission the funding of Masonic
education and leadership training programs and now provides a grant for such purposes. In 2005, the
delegates of the 156th Annual Communication adopted a $30 application fee to be paid to Grand Lodge by all
applicants for the degrees of Masonry and out-of-state affiliations. The Grand Lodge manages different service
bureaus throughout the state and receives reimbursement for expenses incurred with the performance of those
services. The Grand Lodge also manages the investments of its related entities and receives reimbursement
equal to the cost of providing those services. The Grand Lodge is the sole shareholder of the Nob Hill Masonic
Center Inc., and may receive dividends on the profits of this Corporation.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Installation Address

So, who were these men? They were all leaders in their fields – they
all had dreams and a vision of what could be. Just as important, they
were all Masons. They are part of our history. We are proud that they are
a part of our past. We should honor that past – but we cannot live in the
past. We must look forward, as they did, and we must shape our future.

Bruce R. Galloway, Grand Master
Orchestra Video
Wow! Wasn’t that inspiring? Now, when you are asked, “What is
Masonry?” remember this video. Answer that Masonry is talented
individuals coming together in harmony to improve themselves and
create a deep sense of Fraternity and a highly rewarding member
experience. Masonry is dedicated to making a positive impact on society.
Few institutions have the history and traditions of Freemasonry.
Some Masonic scholars will try to trace our beginning back to the
ancient Egyptians. Most will agree that Freemasonry, as we know it
today, began in London 300 years ago. All Masons are proud of
Freemasonry’s historic role in establishing and maintaining the
democracy under which we live, and are grateful to the many talented
Masons that have contributed to our way of life.
Benjamin Franklin and John Hancock were two of 56 signers of the
Declaration of Independence. George Washington, James Monroe,
Andrew Jackson, Theodore Roosevelt, Franklin D. Roosevelt, and Harry
S. Truman were among 14 of our most revered presidents.
Meriwether Lewis, William Clark, and Zebulon M. Pike were the
first explorers of the Louisiana Territory and the upper reaches of the
Mississippi River.
Among far too many military men to mention, are John J Pershing,
George Marshall, Omar Bradley, Douglas MacArthur, and Audie Murphy.
There was Henry Ford from industry, Charles Mayo and Luther
Burbank from science and medicine, and many astronauts and members
of the space program.
John Philip Sousa, Irving Berlin, Gene Autry, Will Rogers, Ernest
Borgnine, Red Skelton, and Duke Ellington were among many
famous entertainers.

As you contemplate those leaders and Masons I just mentioned, ask
yourselves “Are we prepared for the future?” Are we attracting men with
the vision and leadership skills to move our fraternity forward? Sure
we are! We have doctors, lawyers, scientists, businessmen, and skilled
craftsmen in every trade. The issue is whether we will encourage and
then allow these men to lead us into the future.
The theme I have chosen for this year is “Honoring our Past – Shaping
our Future.”
I chose the word honoring very carefully. Our past is what distinguishes
us. It grounds us as Masons. Its teachings have united us and kept us
together. We must, however, honor our past while continually looking to
the future.
I know that there are members who believe that Masonry should
not change. They believe that we should do things the way we always
have. How often have you heard someone say, “That’s not the way it has
always been done?”
Although we joke about change, I’m sure we can all agree that over
time Masonry has changed, and will continue to do so. It has evolved. I
hope you all enjoyed the three special issues of California Freemason
magazine – Yesterday, Today, and Tomorrow. From the very beginning,
Masonry has changed. In some cases because of its movement across
our great nation; in others because of societal evolution, in some cases,
in reaction to external events. Men returned from two wars knowing
camaraderie and fellowship that few will ever experience. They sought
to find it again in Masonry. Those men had significant influence on how
Masonry was practiced for many years.
Young men today may be motivated to join Freemasonry for reasons
different than those of their fathers and grandfathers. That doesn’t
mean that the foundation of Freemasonry, and all that is important to
us has changed, or should change. It does mean, however, that it must
continue to evolve to remain relevant. Men of the greatest generation

80

81

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

were leaders of their lodges and shaped Masonry for many years. We
have a new generation of leaders now. Should we not allow them the
same opportunity to shape Masonry to be relevant in society today?

be more socially- or family-oriented. Some will become Traditional
Observance lodges. No matter what their focus, none are changing
Freemasonry - each is shaping Freemasonry.

A vibrant lodge will constantly ask the questions, “Who are we,
are we focused on those things that are most important to us?” They
execute their plan for today, as they constantly think about their plan
for tomorrow and beyond. They have a vision.

As we move forward, let us build on what has made us great. We are
men who believe in the moral and social virtues; leaders with vision
who are not afraid to try new things or to stop programs that are no
longer relevant. We are men who value diversity and are empowered by
the distinctiveness of our lodges.

Lodges don’t need to make drastic changes. They need to continually
focus on what makes them relevant to their members and the community.
Shaping our future is not the same as changing. Some may say that
that’s a distinction without a difference. I don’t think so. Changing or
adapting can be, and often is, reactionary. There may be times when
that’s necessary, but how much better is it for us to anticipate and shape
our future?
So how do we start? That’s a trick question. There is no beginning and
there is no end. We start where we are now and imagine where we want
to be. We involve new and seasoned members in developing a vision for
our Lodge. We initiate plans to close the gap. Most importantly, we select
motivated leaders.
New lodges are perfect models for what all lodges should consider.
Aside from meeting minimum requirements, they choose motivated
leaders; they decide what is important to its members and what will be
distinctive about their lodge.

The demographics of Freemasonry are changing. That’s not something
to be feared. It should be understood and embraced. Younger men
are knocking on our doors. They may not be coming from Masonic
backgrounds. Their knowledge of Masonry may come from what they
have seen on television or found on the internet. Many probably do not
know anyone in the lodge. Just as important, we do not know them. I’m
pleased to say that lodges are now putting far greater effort into getting
to know prospects. They are also focused on ensuring that a prospect
will be a valuable member of the lodge and an asset to Freemasonry. As
one program for prospects states: first a friend, then a Brother.
As we shape our future, we should consider what our members told
us about their interests: fostering lifelong friendships, learning and
improving ourselves, and making a positive impact on society.
They told us they wanted a rewarding member experience, memorable
and meaningful degrees, strong lodges and halls, and a positive impact
on society.

While some existing lodges struggle, many have begun to look at
what motivates members and have started to create programs to ensure
relevance. Some lodges have annual retreats. It’s an opportunity for
social interaction, a review of programs and accomplishments, and
planning for the future. Some have developed very specific plans for
officer readiness and progression. I’m pleased to say that many lodges
are now placing far greater emphasis on the quality of candidates rather
than quantity.

Lifelong friendships begin when a prospect is invited to lodge events.
He meets members and learns about the culture of the lodge. He begins
to understand Masonry. It continues when he is offered an application.
It is advanced when he is duly and truly prepared for the degrees. An
outstanding ritual experience shows how much a lodge cares about the
candidate and its desire to share knowledge. The mentoring of his coach
will never be forgotten. This leads to true friendship.

Many of the new lodges are a result of Masons seeking relevance and
a Rewarding Member Experience. Some want closer relationships with
their brothers and are forming lodges they intend to keep relatively
small. Some want to focus more on Masonic Education. Others may

We have all heard, or even said, that Masonry makes good men better.
I would say that I believe Masonry gives good men the opportunity to
be better. We provide opportunities through mentoring, encouraging
participation in lodge activities, Masonic education, and encouraging
involvement through leadership roles. Members learn and improve
themselves when they are actively involved.

82

83

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Members tell us that they want to make a positive impact on society.
Interestingly, the young men coming to us today are saying that they
want to be a part of something bigger than themselves. Many lodges
have outstanding local programs. They are involved in community
activities. They have excellent Masonic Outreach programs. They offer
scholarships or have adopted classrooms.

I would like to briefly go back to the video because I believe there
is a message in it for us. Every good orchestra starts with talented
individuals. As individuals they are improving themselves but, just as
importantly, they are improving the orchestra. They are working in
harmony towards a common goal. Leadership brings them together.
Enthusiasm is contagious and spreads internally and externally. Is that
not what we are about as Masons?

Some lodges do not have the resources to do everything they
would like but, working together we can not only shape the future of
Freemasonry, but also the future of some of the most deserving and
vulnerable members of society.
The Grand Master is always asked what his project is for the year.
For the past two years, this year, and for the next several years we have
all committed to support the Masonic charities with which you are so
familiar. Our efforts are devoted to the residents of our Masonic homes
in Union City and Covina and our brothers and their widows needing
assistance while remaining in their communities.
We are also focused on youth. Through the California Masonic
Foundation we continue to offer scholarships to deserving youth who
might otherwise not be able to attend college. We offer scholarships to
well-deserving leaders of our Masonic Youth Groups. Importantly, we
have continued our partnership with Raising A Reader focused on early
childhood literacy.
At the Homes, you would be proud of the work being done on memory
care. As I think about “Honoring Our Past and Shaping Our Future,” it’s
sad to think that some of our residents have lost their past now that
their memories are no longer clear. Alzheimer disease is now the most
feared of all diseases.
If we want a better future, we need to make a difference now. I ask that
you continue your generous support of our Masonic Charities. There
are two urgent issues that need to be addressed. The first is the need
for increased capacity to serve our vulnerable residents desperately in
need of memory care services. The second is expanding our efforts to
engage the families of high-risk elementary school age children around
literacy. Let’s continue to lead in memory care services and support of
our youth.

I would like to leave you with a message I have been giving at all of the
leadership retreats this year. It is a quote from Ralph Waldo Emerson;
“Do not go where the path may lead, go instead where there is no path
and leave a trail.”
I am humbled and honored that you have asked me to serve as Grand
Master this year. I am excited to serve our great Fraternity. Please join
me in Honoring Our Past and Shaping Our Future.

Report of the Senior Grand Warden
Per Capita Recommendation for 2017-18
Stuart A. Wright, Senior Grand Warden
Brethren of the Grand Lodge of California,
I am pleased to present this proposal for the per capita assessment
that will be collected in 2018 to fund the fiscal year operations of Grand
Lodge for the period of November 1, 2018 through October 31, 2019.
I have worked with our leadership team and staff to develop
projections of the income and the necessary expenses for the 2019
fiscal year. Earlier this year, I shared these plans with the Masters and
Wardens who attended our spring leadership retreats. I very much
appreciate the comments and input I received during and following
the retreats.
In preparing a draft budget for the FY2019, I have considered the
factors that will increase per capita, as well as those that will reduce
any necessary increase. The major factors that will increase the per
capita are:
• Membership decline. We project a total loss of 1,354 billable
members. This represents a loss in revenue of $62,961 or $1.43
in per capita. This is an area we all need to heed.
• Fraternal expenses. These expenses are projected to increase by
1.7% or $17,125, which is $0.39 in per capita.
• Appropriations and program expense: I have kept these expenses
at essentially the same level as the previous year. An increase of
less than 1% or $2,670 represents $0.06 in per capita.
• Lodge support in accounting and compliance. We will add one
full-time person to assist lodges with accounting, reporting, tax
preparation, and exempt status protection. Due to the timing,
this is a ¾ increase in 2018, so the additional cost in FY2019 will
be $14,892 or $0.34 in per capita.
• Personnel costs. Wages are held to a 3% increase. Health
insurance is expected to increase 6%. Total personnel cost
increases, not including the above position, of $52,189 represent
$1.19 in per capita.

• Non-labor expense inflation. Items subject to inflation are
expected to increase by 2% representing $6,346 or $0.14 in
per capita.
Per capita would need to increase by $3.55 to cover the effect of all
of these factors. With an increase in the dividend from the Nob Hill
Masonic Center and slight increases in investment and other income,
the necessary per capita increase can be lowered by $1.30 to $2.25.

Report of the Grand Treasurer
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethren All:
In my second address to you as your Grand Treasurer, I am again
pleased to report to you that the overall financial health of our Grand
Lodge and related entities remains strong. We continue to benefit from
the efforts and expertise of so many brothers volunteering their time
as Board Members and Committee Members, as well as the expertise of
our entire Grand Lodge financial team led by CFO Tom Boyer, Controller
Maribel Pasamic, Director of Financial Planning Khalil Sweidy, and Very
Worshipful Allan Casalou, our Grand Secretary.
The Audit Committee has again chosen to work with Moss Adams as
our outside auditor to ensure that our financial statement audits for all
of our Grand Lodge entities continue to go smoothly. As of our last fiscal
year ending October 31, 2016, each of our entities continued to receive
a clean audit opinion and were informed that our internal controls
remain effective.
The Finance Committee continues to work with our Deputy Grand
Master and Senior Grand Warden each year to provide wise and
timely counsel in the preparation of their annual budgets and per
capita determinations.
The Insurance Committee has worked tirelessly in their detailed
review of our complex insurance needs for not only our Grand
Lodge entities but also for our lodges and Hall Associations. They
continue to review ongoing claims to ensure an optimal result for the
benefit of the Craft and to look for ways to do all of this in the most
cost-efficient manner.
The Investment Committee remains steadfast in its ongoing efforts
to monitor the economic factors which impact our portfolio. In their
evaluation of our investment policies they continue to recommend
that 4.5% of our investment portfolio be distributed to fund operating
budgets, which will also work to preserve and grow our overall
portfolio for future use. And during this last Grand Lodge year, they
have engaged the firm NEPC as our new investment advisor to provide
timely analysis and recommendations on our various fund managers.
This has resulted in minor modifications to our asset allocations which
were approved by each of our constitutional boards.

I have reported increases and very little change to the investments
of each of our entities, but it is also noteworthy that in aggregate our
Master Trust has increased $85,744,008 or 9.05% net of distributions for
the operations for all of our entities. The Master Trust has surpassed a
major milestone by breaking the billion-dollar mark and now stands at
$1,032,680,932 as of July 31, 2017. The return on investment for the year
to date is 8.3% and since inception of our Master Trust in 1995 it is 7.7%.
In 1992, our Grand Lodge created an Endowment Fund to be funded
each year by the budget surpluses of each Grand Master. Since that
time the Endowment Fund has grown to $2,453,304 as of July 31, 2017.

Heisner. This same Endowment Fund will now provide $100,894 for the
budget of Right Worshipful Galloway in the fiscal year ending October
31, 2018 compared to the amount of $99,203 for the current fiscal year.

Proceedings of the

As previously mentioned our participation in the Grand Lodge Life
Membership Funds and also the Grand Lodge General Investments
Fund has increased over the last year providing Lodges a much needed
option in their investment strategies. As of July 31, 2017 we have 38
lodges participating in the Life Membership Master Fund with a value
of $1,408,214 and we have seven lodges participating in the Lodge
Investments Master Fund with a value of $1,676,351.
Unfortunately, we continue to have lodges and hall associations
experiencing challenges with budgets, investments, payroll matters,
tax filings, and general accounting matters. I continue to encourage not
only those facing these challenges but all lodges and hall associations
to reach out to your District Inspector for guidance. These hardworking
men are knowledgeable in the many resources available to you through
our Grand Lodge such as Intacct training, tax preparation services,
payroll services, investment guidance, audit guidance, real estate
matters, and many others. In utilizing these services and the expertise
of our Grand Lodge staff, you will be able to focus more of your attention
on practicing Masonry within your lodge and your community.
I would also like to encourage you to begin your budget discussions
as early as possible with all of the key people in your lodge such as your
prospective Wardens, Treasurer, Secretary, Trustees, Hall Association
Directors, and those with experience in such matters. Discuss your
budgets openly and frequently so that the finances of your lodge do not
become one of the mysteries of Freemasonry.
Lastly, I would like to thank all of you for the opportunity to continue
to serve you as Grand Treasurer. I enjoy working on your behalf with so
many caring and dedicated individuals. I would especially like to thank
my friend, Very Worshipful Allan Casalou, for his extensive business
knowledge and for his tireless efforts which continue to bring increased
efficiency and professionalism into the operations of our Grand Lodge
and related entities for the benefit of all California Masons.
Respectfully submitted by,
Arthur L. Salazar Jr., Grand Treasurer

Report of the Grand Secretary
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Members of the Grand Lodge:
In my 10th report as your Grand Secretary, I am pleased to say that
Masonry in California is thriving, thanks to our forward-looking leaders
and devoted members. California Masons are actively working to make a
difference – in our homes, lodges, communities, and the world. Thanks to
our brothers’ dedication and collaboration, our jurisdiction is providing
a Masonic experience that not only touches lives, but transforms them.
MEMBERSHIP INFORMATION
As of June 30, 2017, we had 48,196 active Masons, including 2,978
Entered Apprentice Masons and 908 Fellow Crafts. More than 2,150
are newly initiated, affiliated, or restored brothers. This is balanced by
3,860 losses, which lowers our total membership by three percent since
last year.
We learned that some 1,500 brothers were suspended for
nonpayment of dues over the past year – constituting 90 percent of
the total membership decline – and that nearly 4,000 were suspended
over the past two years. Very few have been restored. When contacted
these brothers often say they simply lost their connection with the
lodge and many wish to be reinstated. We are therefore initiating a
campaign to reconnect suspended brothers to the fraternity. By better
understanding their experiences, we hope to improve processes and
reduce suspensions. Full details will be shared at the 2018 Secretary
and Treasurer Retreats; progress will be reviewed during Master and
Wardens Retreats.
Our California Masonic family also includes 24,271 widows. They
receive Grand Lodge communications throughout the year, including
the California Freemason magazine, and I receive grateful responses in
return. I encourage every lodge to maintain contact with their widows
to offer fellowship and support.
A detailed report of membership activity, by-law amendments, life
memberships, and veterans’ awards will be included in my written
report in the Proceedings.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Proceedings of the

PROGRAMS AND SERVICES
The 2020 Fraternity Plan calls for strong lodges and halls. We are
helping lodges create sound administrative, financial, and operating
plans; building strong new lodges; and strengthening lodge leadership.
More than ever before, we’re helping lodges reduce administrative
burdens and prioritize the member experience.
Member Services
Our Member Services team provides core support to lodges and
members – from standard transactions to forming new lodges and
everything in between. They processed nearly 7,000 requests this
year, completing more than 90 percent on the first day with an
average completion time of 90 minutes. They handled more than 1,200
background checks and nearly 1,100 awards and recognitions. They
processed by-law amendments and dispensations, and guided lodges
through consolidation.
Leadership retreat attendance reached an all-time high this year
with over 1,000 participants. Nearly 540 officers attended the Masters
and Wardens Retreats – our largest turnout yet. Member Services
administered these and other statewide events, processing more than
3,500 registrations. They also provided crucial hands-on support,
including registration, vendor relations, and concierge services.
Member Services provides invaluable assistance to brothers forming
new lodges as well. This year, 35 groups of Masons proposed new
lodges. Six were granted dispensations, one is progressing towards
dispensation, three are preparing to submit a letter of intent, and seven
are applying for charters. I will give a full report on charters tomorrow.
Financial Services
The Financial Services team provides accounting, reporting, budget
and audit support for Grand Lodge and our related entities. Additionally,
they support lodges and halls in fulfilling their fiduciary duties to the
fraternity and government, offering business and financial services
through a variety of supportive programs and resources.

101

They continued to help lodges implement and utilize Intacct, our
accounting and reporting system. Intacct is being used or tested by 247
lodges and 125 halls, greatly reducing administrative tasks. Financial
Services offers an Intacct support hotline and prepares annual lodge
financial reports, which are provided to inspectors.
This year Financial Services prepared and filed 380 tax returns for
lodges, halls, and Masonic Homes residents. They restored tax-exempt
status to 29 lodges, saving $11,660 in tax penalties, and achieved
retroactive reinstatement for Franklin Hall, avoiding taxation on the
building’s sale. Nine lodges are pending reinstatement, and tax penalty
notices have significantly decreased overall.
Next year, I hope more lodges will take advantage of these resources,
especially to enroll in Intacct if the lodge is not already. We need to
be united in our efforts to manage the organization as effectively as
possible. When we work together, even complex financial matters can
be managed efficiently and effectively.
Real Estate Services
We continue to expand real estate services, including property
improvement consultations, sales, purchases, and leases, as well as
advice on building operations, insurance, hall valuations, appraisals,
and routine and preventive maintenance. Real estate services manages
Grand Lodge-owned properties, including halls in Columbia, Benicia,
Monrovia, and Moreno Valley and supports the important work of the
Masonic Properties Committee, which reviews applications from lodges
and halls regarding Masonic properties.
Legal Services
Our Legal services team supports lodges and consults with halls
when appropriate. This year they helped resolve business disputes,
litigation, insurance claims, and other matters. They consulted with
hall associations on leases and created hall use agreement templates to
simplify administration.
Legal services facilitates estate settlements for the California Masonic
Foundation and Masonic Homes of California. This year, they helped
administer more than $6.6 million in planned gifts. They also facilitated
more than 44 Masonic trial matters, completing 26.

102

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Proceedings of the

103

Communications

Fundraising

Our
Communications
team
provides
a
comprehensive
communications portfolio for our fraternity, including websites, social
media, a weekly e-newsletter, a monthly leadership e-newsletter, and
the bimonthly California Freemason magazine.

Annual Fund efforts have been very successful this year. We raised
more than $8 million, including $1.3 million in Annual Fund gifts and
$7 million in realized planned gifts. Our fundraising team’s emphasis
on leadership-level giving to the Annual Fund resulted in more Grand
Master Circle level and Anniversary Level donors.

Our 2017 video, “Celebrating the Masonic Homes of California,” won
an industry award from the Association of Media and Publishing. Our
philanthropic “Making a Profound Impact” video garnered more than
100,000 views since its August 2017 release and has been shared more
than 2,000 times. California Freemason magazine is a finalist in four
categories of the Folio Awards – a prestigious editorial, design, and
marketing competition.
In 2017, we introduced the California Freemason Publication
Committee to guide strategic direction of our magazine. Brothers Dago
Rodriquez, Emanuel Rose, Russ Hennings, Ian Laurelin, and James
Tucker met quarterly to review progress and plan future editions.
This year, they undertook a significant project – creating a 90-page
commemorative edition titled “300 Years of Freemasonry,” which
explores the progression of the fraternity from its foundation to today.
This elegant book is packaged in a gold foil-embellished, soft-touch
keepsake box, which is handcrafted, hand-numbered, and includes an
exclusive 300th anniversary commemorative coin. Only 1,000 copies
are available. Purchase yours at the Communications booth in the
Exhibition Hall, or reserve a copy online. I thank the committee for
their excellent work this year.
More than 200 lodges and 5,000 brothers are using the lodge app,
which allows members to stay connected on a secure mobile platform.
Many lodges collect payments through the app, collectively processing
thousands of dollars each month.
Lodge websites are often the first impression prospective members,
the community, and the media have of a lodge, so it is essential for
websites to be professional, engaging, and informative. This year, Grand
Lodge offered lodges a website template and provided training and
support for implementation. More than 60 lodges have utilized these
templates, and more sites are in development. For information about
website templates, visit the Communications booth.

This year we welcomed 13 new members to the Cornerstone Society,
a special group of donors who include the fraternity in their wills or
estate plans. More than 177 living Cornerstone Society members are
ensuring that fraternal relief and community support will endure for
future generations.
Through Masons4Mitts, we continued to support our communities by
purchasing baseball mitts for underprivileged children associated with
the San Francisco Giants, Los Angeles Dodgers, and San Diego Padres.
Our brothers raised more than $140,000, this year reaching more than
7,000 children. Masons4Mitts is a great community engagement tool:
More than 1,100 brothers and guests attended Masons Night at Major
League Baseball ballparks where thousands of people experienced
our check presentations in person and through radio and television
coverage. Thank you to the teams and captains who continue this
program’s success.
I personally want to thank every Mason who participated in our
fundraising efforts this year. Together, we have made a huge impact –
and thanks to your gifts, we will continue to do so.
RECOGNITION OF FOREIGN GRAND LODGES
It is my responsibility to inform the Grand Master of matters
pertaining to foreign grand lodge recognition and to present to you, in
the form of a motion, the recognition of certain grand lodges that meet
our criteria.
This year, we received recognition requests from grand lodges
in Brazil, Eastern Europe, and two Mexican states. The Executive
Committee agreed that we should strengthen relationships with these
grand lodges to better understand their practices before agreeing
to mutual recognition. This year, we have been invited to attend the
Confederation of Regular Grand Lodges in Mexico, which will provide
an opportunity to deepen our connections with state grand lodges
in Mexico.

104

105

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

California Masons are fortunate to enjoy close relationships with
grand lodges in and near our state and these relationships afford unique
opportunities for you and me. Attend a Prince Hall lodge and you will
experience a variation of our own ritual. You may witness the Emulation
Rite by visiting lodges under the Grand Lodge of Iran in Exile, and you
can witness the first three degrees of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish
Rite just across the border in Mexico. I encourage you to take advantage
of these opportunities whenever you can.

Lastly, I want to thank our Grand Master, Most Worshipful Brother
John R. Heisner, who has led our fraternity with a steady hand, a sharp
mind, and a good heart. He set the example of leadership for all of us.
He kept us focused on our goals, made us accountable for our work,
recognized us for our achievements, and allowed us to have fun in the
process. I’ve grown as a man and a leader under him. Thank you, Most
Worshipful, for your excellent leadership and your friendship; and
thank you for your service to our Craft.

It is also important to take stock of the strong public relationships
we have nurtured. In addition to our current strong relationships with
Major League Baseball teams through Masons4Mitts, next year we will
also partner with the Anaheim Angels.

And thank you, my brothers, for the opportunity to serve and work
with you.

We look forward to marking our 10th year of our partnership with
UCLA, focused on Freemasonry and civil society. Thanks to our support,
hundreds of academic researchers have pursued high-level Masonic
scholarship that has informed our members. In April, we will sponsor
the 6th International Conference on Freemasonry at UCLA.
The California Department of Education views the Masons of
California as a valuable ally in supporting public education. And, we
have built a strong partnership with national literacy organization
Raising A Reader, helping families build literacy habits at home.
We are proud of these relationships, which are helping to preserve the
excellent reputation of the Masons of California. By sharing our good
work, we are enabling our members to feel a sense of accomplishment
and helping good men learn about the fraternity.
ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS
As I conclude my report, I wish to extend my sincere gratitude to
the Lodge Secretaries and Assistant Secretaries whose dedicated work
is the backbone of our jurisdiction. I also wish to thank our Assistant
Grand Lecturers and District Inspectors who, in addition to their ritual
duties, provide invaluable administrative support throughout the year.
I am blessed to work with a team of true professionals in our Grand
Lodge office, all of whom care deeply about our Fraternity and support
our mission with their dedicated service. I thank them all for their
commitment and good work.

Respectfully submitted by,
Allan L. Casalou, Grand Secretary

On February 7, 2017, the charter for Pomona Lodge No. 246, was
suspended and arrested. A motion was made, seconded, and adopted
to revoke the charter for Pomona Lodge No. 246. The Lodge will be
dissolved in accordance with the California Masonic Code, and the
assets thereof, other than the lodge’s Life Membership Fund, will be
held and used for the establishment of new lodges.
