Report of the Grand Lecturer
Most Worshipful and Members of the Grand Lodge:
The CMC requires that I provide you with a detailed accounting of
the past year’s activities and the status of the ritual in our jurisdiction.
During this Grand Lodge Masonic term, I continued to hold monthly
conference calls with the members of the Ritual Committee and the
Grand Secretary and his staff. With the reorganization of the Lodge
Support Committee (LSC), which now includes all nine Assistant Grand
Lecturers, a portion of the monthly conference calls were set aside for
use by the LSC Chairman.
From my visitations, and reports to me from the Assistant Grand
Lecturers and others, the overall quality of our ritual remains satisfactory.
There are some lodges where excellent ritual quality is the norm, while
other lodges demonstrate just the opposite. The difference between the
two seems to be the degree to which the leadership of each lodge has
discovered the happy medium between the time spent on ritual and the
time spent on social activities.
I was very impressed with the ritual exemplifications provided by the
several Divisions where the host AGLs provided a team of their very
best ritualists to exemplify the work. There was no doubt that those who
witnessed the events walked away with a very memorable ritual and
membership experience. The impact the ritual teams had upon those
in attendance will not be forgotten.
And speaking of memorable ritual experiences, I call your attention
to two significant events of ritual excellence as well as outstanding
membership experience. I am talking about the continued efforts by
the ritual team from the Manlalakbay Na Gurong Masons (a.k.a. MGM
or Traveling Masons), as well as the three ritual teams that comprised
this year’s very first annual Masonathon held by Division 9 Masons in
San Diego.
Both of those groups provided wonderful examples of outstanding
ritual and memorable membership experiences. Both groups combined
outstanding degree conferrals with some fantastic social events. The
events do require detailed planning and some serious commitment by
the participant; however, the results are so very beneficial to our Craft
and should be emulated by other Divisions and/or Districts.

134

135

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

I held two Inspector Ritual conferences and five Master Mason ritual
schools. During these sessions, we reviewed the manner in which we
confer all three degrees, the proficiencies, the Master’s lectures, the
Institution of New Lodges ceremony, the Installation ritual, and the new
Golden Veteran’s Award ceremony; all with an eye on how to improve
membership experience from the point of view of the candidate, the
sideliner, and the lodge officer.

There were 77 competitions held statewide and the winners are
as follows:

My personal theme for this year was “Ritual is the language of unity,”
which was intended to remind us of the many ways our ritual unites us.
This special kind of unity can be seen in our brethren who fought for
their respective countries and, while in prisoner of war camps, found
some precious time to meet brothers, make good men into Masons, and
- in a few cases - establish a lodge within their camps where the Ritual
maintained their special unity.
One such lodge was formed inside Hut 6 in a Nazi concentration
camp. More than 100 prisoners were in Hut 6, and locked up nearly
around the clock—allowed to leave only for a half-hour walk per day,
under supervision. The prisoners were forced to work under dreadful
conditions. Even in those terrible conditions, our brethren found
precious space and time to use their Ritual to unite as Masons and on
November 15, 1943, to start a lodge inside the Hut called Loge Liberté
Chérie (Cherished Liberty Lodge). It should be noted that a Catholic
priest would stand outside the door in order to allow the brethren to
hold their meetings and protect their secrecy. You see, even under those
perilous times our brethren utilized our ritual as the language of unity
in order to help survive the ravages of war; an example my brethren
worthy of all imitation.
We need to remember that the Ritual is not the last goal in Masonry,
but it is a very important fairway along which Masons may travel in
search of perfection. While the Masonic experience must never end
with the Ritual, it must always begin there. Upon the quality of the
beginning depends the success of the ending, and we should strive to
balance Ritual work with personal and social development.
In our continuing effort to ensure a meaningful and rewarding
Masonic experience, we held an individual Ritual Competition wherein
one individual from each Division was recognized as their best Ritualist
in the delivery of all three Charges. Here are the results.

• Division 1 (06 competitions) - Jonathan Chan, Crocker Lodge
No. 212, No. 361854
• Division 2 (05 competitions) - G. Sean Metroka, Nevada Lodge
No. 13, No. 19592
• Division 3 (13 competitions) - Daren Miller, Oakland Durant
Rockridge Lodge No. 188, No. 351999
• Division 4 (11 competitions) - Tommy Farr, Hornitos Lodge
No. 98, No. 13642
• Division 5 (05 competitions) – Thomas Darnell, Caledonia
No. 486, No. 92175
• Division 6 (19 competitions) - Jason Palazzolo, Downey United
No. 220, No. 350471
• Division 7 (13 competitions) - Kelly Gilliam, Reseda Lodge
No. 666, No. 336852
• Division 8 (01 competition) - Robert Carrico, Temecula Catalina

• Division 9 (06 competitions) – Brandon E. Cuenca, Penrhyn

It should be noted the average Masonic tenure for the competitors
was 15 years. When you remove the three most tenured competitors, the
average tenure for the remaining six wining competitors was two years.
Congratulations to all of this year’s winners!
I would also like to take this opportunity to thank every Officers
Coach and Inspector for their tireless, and often unrewarded, efforts to
work with the Craft to improve the Ritual experience in general and our
members’ experiences in particular.

The world needs to find a way to secure its moral anchor into a firm
foundation of civility, and today, more than at any other time, we have
been called upon to lead the way. Learn from our Masonic teachers,
practice your Ritual at home, rehearse your Ritual in lodge, hold firm
to your anchor to civility, share with others what you have learned,
practice and teach civility to all those around you, and set the example
for the world to follow.

Respectfully submitted by,
Jack M. Rose, Grand Lecturer

Appendix G

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

141

Grand Chaplain
Inspirational Message
There was a quote in a recent issue of California Freemason magazine
that said, “The greatest secret of Freemasonry is finding out who you
really are.” This stuck me as a perfect theme for this message.
Masonry is, at its heart, a lifelong journey in self-improvement that
ultimately improves not only each Mason, but eventually his family, his
lodge, and society in general.
This very personal journey is different for all of us, with different
paths, stops, and goals. To make this journey effective takes preparation,
thoughtful introspection, and - above all - hard work. Our symbolic
working tools provide us with great guides for our journey in selfimprovement.
How can we efficiently use these precious tools and implements?
While reading a book written by Steven Covey, a non-Mason, entitled
“Seven Habits of Highly Effective People,” I realized that it provides a
way of putting Masonry into practice.
The book is based on developing and centering our attitudes and
actions through our character and morals, not on personality. A
personality-centered person may be manipulative and their actions can
result in bad feelings in others and failure to achieve desired goals. A
principle-centered person develops pathways for changing himself and
the way he views the world around him.
The text refers to values based on integrity, humility, fidelity,
temperance, courage, justice, patience, industry, simplicity, modesty, and
the Golden Rule. Sound familiar? This is very similar to another quote
from the same issue of California Freemason magazine on truth: “Stay
true to our personal code of conduct and ethics – honoring integrity,
personal responsibility, and the continuous pursuit of knowledge.” The
values that govern our behavior ultimately determine the results of
our endeavors as well as determining who we are. By developing these
habits I believe we can increase the understanding and knowledge of
our working tools and use them more efficiently.
Although Mr. Covey refers to seven habits I will concentrate on the
first three which center on the self-development so important to us
as Masons.

142

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

143

Habit 1 - Be Proactive

Habit 2 - Begin With The End In Mind

What distinguishes us from all other animals is our ability to examine
our own character and to decide how to view ourselves and our
situations. We can control our own effectiveness.

This is an incredibly important habit to develop. In Masonry we have
been asked to develop a mission or vision of what we want to become
and use our conscience and our symbolic tools to decide how we will be
guided to those ends.

In order to be effective, a person must be proactive. A reactive person
feels and acts as if he were a victim but a proactive person will recognize
that he has responsibility or more accurately “response-ability.” This
is the ability to choose how you will respond to a given stimulus or
situation. It is the opposite of a knee-jerk reaction. About 20 years ago
we were on a bus in Ireland. One of the men in our party was sitting next
to a young Irishman who immediately began to rant about a political
situation in the US. Our friend very calmly spoke to the young man about
the situation and provided a different perspective to the young man’s.
The confrontation soon turned into a quiet conversation. Our friend’s
patience and demeanor influenced the young man and he positively
impressed the other members in our group who were listening.
We can be much more productive in an angry situation by employing
a responsible and calm reaction to confrontation, utilizing patience and
self-control instead of reciprocating an equally angry response. How we
respond is our choice. This is “response-ability.”
In order to be proactive people we must focus on situations we can do
something about. We waste our time and energy if we dwell on things
we cannot influence. Reactive people react in a way that decreases their
influence by blaming others or circumstances. A proactive person will
see how he can contribute to helping with a situation.
Think of the difference it would make if we thought “What can I
do to help?” instead of “I won’t do anything about that.” How we view
ourselves and ensuring that our responses match our values are very
valuable and productive tools.

Through deep thought and self-examination we should carefully
develop our goals. Are our goals principle-centered? Our activities and
efforts should begin with that end in mind.
We can’t let our business and daily distractions be in the way of
these goals. It reminds me of the story about the guy that was busily
driving from San Diego to Phoenix when he suddenly realized what
he wanted was in San Francisco. Some good basic questions for all our
activities are:
• What am I trying to accomplish?
• What I am doing get there?
• Do these activities and goals coincide with my values?
Habit 3. Put First Things First
In order to manage ourselves effectively, we must put first things first.
We must have the self-discipline to prioritize our everyday actions
based on what is most important, not on what is urgent at the moment.
This habit puts in action what we plan to do to realize the goals
we developed in Habit 2 (Begin with the End in Mind). This requires
discipline and willpower to execute our priorities on a daily basis.
At times it requires doing something we really do not want to do, such
as taking that two mile walk to stay in shape or turning off the television
to do some critical reading that will be beneficial to our career or lodge
activities. Our focus needs to be centered on those values we deem
important and we must plan ahead so we are not always in crisis mode.
Remember that 80% of our results comes from 20% of our time. Mr.
Covey had a perfect summation for this habit, “The challenge is not to
manage time, but to manage ourselves.”

• Be Proactive.
• Begin With the End in Mind.
• Put First Things First.
These are three habits I have tried to use to improve myself by
incorporating them into my life and Masonry. These are life habits
that, if developed, will help us to be more aware of ourselves. Try these
principles and use them as guidelines for your daily life and you will
become a better man, better husband, better parent, better employee,
and better citizen – improving mankind one person at a time.

Grand Oration
Good morning, brethren.
Today, each of us has a job to do. My job is to talk and yours is to
listen. The challenge is for me to finish my job before you are finished
with yours.
Let me begin by telling you an old story that has been told time and
time again but seems appropriate for this Annual Communication. The
story goes that at the latter part of the first century A.D., there was an
old Rabbi named Akiva ben Yosef. One day, he was walking along the Sea
of Galilee on his way home to Capernaum. It was late in the afternoon
and like the good Jew that he was, Rabbi Akiva was deep in thought
pondering and meditating upon the scriptures and his purpose in life.
He was so focused that he didn’t realize that he had gone astray and
instead of being at the gates of Capernaum, he found himself in front of
the large gate of a Roman fortress.
By this time, the sun had gone down and as Rabbi Akiva stood in front
of the gate realizing what had happened, he heard a loud voice coming
down from above the gate. It was the voice of a Roman guard standing
on the top of the wall. The guard shouted down to this stranger: “Who
are you? What are you doing here?”
The Rabbi was startled and could only respond with, “What?” Again,
the guard called out, “Who are you? What are you doing here?”
Rabbi Akiva had a few moments to gather his thoughts and he shouted
back at the Roman Guard, “How much do you get paid to ask me
these questions?”
The guard was now confused. Why would this stranger ask such
a question in response? After a few moments of silence, he said, “Two
drachmas per week!” To this Rabbi Akiva responded with intense
conviction: “I’ll pay you double if you stand outside of my house and ask
me those same questions every morning.”
Today, my brothers, I ask those questions to you. Who are you and
what are you doing here?

This year, we are celebrating a milestone: 300 years of Freemasonry.
This past Grand Lodge year was a celebration of our 300 years in
existence from 1717 to 2017. Three hundred years is certainly a long
time. We also know that our Craft is even older than that. I don’t know of
any fraternal organization or any organization that has lasted this long.
Well, maybe the church. Our Fraternity has evolved with the times and
I am happy to say that the changes that have occurred in our Fraternity
have kept up with the times, and they have all been good.

In its preamble, it proclaimed that the “inherent dignity and the
equal and inalienable rights of all members of the human family is the
foundation of freedom, justice, and peace in the world.”

As you reach a milestone in your life, I think it is worth asking
these two questions: Who are you and what are you doing here? As
you go through life, you will undoubtedly have different answers to
these questions, and your answers will depend on your experiences
and circumstances.
Well, as Freemasons, we have reached a milestone. Perhaps we should
ask: Who are we, and what are we doing here?
I will say that throughout this year, our Most Worshipful Grand Master
has given us the answers. Your Grand Lodge has traveled all over this
state, this country and beyond. Those of us who have been blessed to be
able to tag along have seen and heard answers to these two questions.
Today, I will try to answer these questions based on what I’ve experienced
and hope that you will agree with me.
The first question deals with our identity: Who are we? What do we
stand for and what do we represent?
During what I call our “installation season,” our Most Worshipful
Grand Master installed the officers of many, many lodges. In his address
to Masons and guests after each installation, our Grand Master made
a point to include the fact that Freemasonry stands for freedom and
human rights.
Last December, our Grand Master pointed this out upon the
anniversary of the proclamation of the Universal Declaration of Human
Rights. Not long after World War II, this landmark document was drafted
by the United Nations Human Rights Commission, which was chaired
by our former first lady, Eleanor Roosevelt, wife of our brother Franklin
Delano Roosevelt.

Article 1 says: “All human beings are born free and equal in dignity
and rights. They are endowed with reason and conscience and should
act towards one another in a spirit of brotherhood.”
Article 2 says: “Everyone is entitled to all the rights and freedoms set
forth in this Declaration, without distinction of any kind, such as race,
color, sex, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social
origin, property, birth or other status.”
Now, does that sound familiar? Isn’t that what Freemasonry stands
for? Isn’t that what we want to identify with in our daily lives? Isn’t this
what we want to protect?
This year, we were privileged to attend the California Masonic
Symposium on the Moscow archives. It was an eye opener to learn
how Nazism, a power of evil in this world, began a reign of tyranny
by seizing the Masonic records of lodges in France, the Netherlands,
Belgium, and other countries in Europe. They captured 27,000 dossiers
of Masonic history. Imagine that. At that time, it was very dangerous to
be identified as a Mason and to have your name listed in the archives of
the lodge. It was a horrific time in the world when freedom was at stake.
Yet, we learned that there were many Masons who, having heard of this
atrocity, hid the records of their lodges and prevented the Nazis from
confiscating them.
If you consider the many countries in the world who have struggled
for freedom and human rights, I bet that in each of those struggles you
will find Freemasonry represented. Only when freedom is present can
Freemasonry progress. Without freedom and without us fighting for
freedom, our Fraternity will not survive. My brothers, we should ever be
vigilant in protecting our freedom and our God-given human rights. This
is our identity.
What I have seen this year during our Grand Master’s travels up
and down this great state is the uniqueness of our fraternity especially
in today’s social and political climate. Freemasonry, as a universal
brotherhood, is an organization unique in these times of strong
differences of opinions, beliefs, schisms, and dissentions. Masonry

allows men of divergent opinions to meet in peace and harmony as a
basic ideal. A lodge is not just a building but is the people who band
together as fraternal brothers. In the lodges that we visited, large and
small, you can immediately see who is the lodge. People of all ages,
backgrounds, careers, and cultural diversity make up the lodge. In all of
these visits, we saw what Freemasonry is truly about. All were seated
in the lodge “on the level” as brothers. The lodge is where we learn and
practice brotherhood. We appreciate our differences and we learn to
focus on what unites us. Yes, Freemasonry is a unifying force for good in

But all their uprisings were local in scope. Waged by a divided people,

This year, our Grand Master had the opportunity to represent us, the
California Grand Lodge, during the Annual Communication of the Grand
Lodge of the Philippines. He and a host of others traveled across the

I mention this because in its travels up and down this state, this Grand
Lodge has witnessed the vibrancy, the vitality, and the enthusiasm of the
“Filipino Lodges” in the state. I have heard the question many times:
why is Freemasonry such a magnet for the Filipino community? Let me
propose one possible answer.
The colonial history of the Philippines is sometimes described as
“300 years in the convent and 50 years in Hollywood.” Three hundred
years under Spanish rule and 50 years under American rule. We all
know the unifying role that our fraternity played in the formation of
the United States and its struggle for independence from Great Britain.
We have George Washington, Benjamin Franklin, and other Masonic
heroes of the revolution. Well, the Philippines also had Masonic heroes
during their struggle for independence from Spain. They had Jose Rizal,
Graciano Lopez-Jaena, Antonio Luna, Marcelo del Pilar and others.
These Masons were the catalysts that supported the Philippine struggle
for independence from Spain.
Let me give you some context. During the time of Spanish rule, the
Philippines were essentially a collection of divided tribes, a people
without a sense of nationhood. They did not look at themselves as
Filipinos, but people from different provinces or regions in the country.
So, there were the Tagalogs from one region, the Pampangueños from
another; the Ilocanos from one province, the Visayans from another,
and so on. They belonged to the same racial stock and shared a common
grievance against their colonizer, but did not embrace each other

This is where Masonry comes in. The Filipino Masons saw the unifying
value of Masonry. They had come from different regions and provinces
of the country – Jose Rizal was from Laguna, Graciano Lopez-Jaena from
Iloilo, Marcelo del Pilar from Bulacan, Antonio Luna from Ilocos and so
on but inside the lodge all their regional differences were forgotten; they
all sat in lodge and mingled together as brothers, as Filipinos.
Marcelo del Pilar expressed it perfectly when he wrote:
“Masonry has consecrated its efforts to the task of uniting all men
in brotherhood, erasing the differences of country, race and color, of
banishing war, replacing the din of arms and clanking of chains with the
sound of work and industry.”
My friends, that is why Filipinos gravitate to Masonry. In the confines
of the lodge, a true brotherhood exists and provincial differences are
forgotten. Unity exists!
I am a third-generation Filipino Mason. I became a Mason in California,
not in a Filipino lodge, but a lodge with men from many backgrounds and
cultures. I became the first Filipino Master of my lodge but I always felt
that my brothers saw me not as a Filipino Mason but a brother Mason
unified by our common commitment to the principles of Freemasonry.
Masonry’s unifying force exists not only in the Philippines but also in
our great state of California and everywhere our gentle Craft is allowed
to flourish.
So, what are we doing here? What is our purpose as Masons?
My answer is simply this. Once we know who we are and what we
are, then isn’t it our purpose to conduct ourselves in all things so that
our identity will be known to others. We are here to reflect the tenets of
Freemasonry and be a beacon to the world.

Carry-Over Legislation from 2016

Resolution No. 16-04
Allows Additional Exception to Ballot Secrecy
The proponents of this Resolution seek to allow an exception to the
rule on ballot secrecy when reporting, preparing, investigating and/or
adjudicating charges of alleged unmasonic conduct relating to a ballot.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, Section 804.450 of the California Masonic Code, in the
case of an unfavorable ballot, only allows a member to divulge his vote
on a ballot, or to assign reasons for such vote, if it be known, to the
Master for the purpose of correcting a mistake; and
WHEREAS, unmasonic conduct under California Masonic Code
Section 1401.010, subsection G.3.g includes improper use of ballot; and
WHEREAS, there have been Masonic trials in which instances
of improper of use of the ballot box have been alleged against
Wardens and Masters, but the charges could not be proven because of
Section 804.450.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 804.450 of the
California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§804.450. BALLOT SECRECY.
Except for the three officers whose duty it is to examine the ballot
box, no one is entitled to know the number of votes cast for or against
an applicant. There shall be no discussion regarding an unfavorable
ballot. No member of a lodge shall be required, requested, or allowed to
divulge his vote upon a ballot, or to assign reasons for such vote, if it be
known, except to the Master for the purpose of correcting a mistake. The
foregoing notwithstanding, such discussion or disclosure is permitted
when reporting, preparing, investigating, and/or adjudicating charges
of alleged unmasonic conduct relating to a ballot.

158

Proceedings of the

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
Section 804.450 of the California Masonic Code sets forth this
Grand Lodge’s general rule on ballot secrecy: no discussion may be
had regarding an unfavorable ballot, and no member of a lodge may
be required, requested, or allowed to divulge his vote upon a ballot or
assign reasons for his vote. Section 804.450 also provides one exception
to this general rule: specifically, a member may divulge his vote, and
assign reasons for his vote, solely to the Master for the purpose of
correcting a mistake.
This Grand Lodge’s general rule on ballot secrecy originated from
Masonic jurist Brother Albert J. Mackey’s writings on the subject.
Brother Mackey’s rule on ballot secrecy, from his “A Textbook of
Masonic Jurisprudence,” provides that “no inquiry on [a member’s vote]
can be entertained [and that] no information [on a member’s vote]
can be received” while also stating that it is “wrong, in the exercise of
[balloting], for [a member] to be influenced by [improper motives]”
such as pique or prejudice.
Although it would still, at times, use Mackey’s rule as a reference, this
Grand Lodge adopted its own general rule on ballot secrecy in 1851
by way of a standing resolution to its first Constitution. That standing
resolution provided that “no member of a lodge can be required to
divulge his vote on balloting for a candidate for the degrees of Masonry,
or for membership, nor to assign reasons for his vote, if known.”
No exception to our Grand Lodge’s general rule on ballot secrecy
then existed.
This Grand Lodge did not create an exception to its general rule
on ballot secrecy until 1874, when the Grand Lodge adopted an
amended and re-stated version of its Constitution at the 1874 Annual
Communication. Part V, Article II, Section 2 of the 1874 Constitution
provided as follows: “No member of a lodge shall be required to divulge
his vote upon a ballot for affiliation, or for the degrees of Masonry; nor
to assign reasons for such vote, if it be known except to the Master for
the purpose of correcting a mistake.”
Although the language of the general rule on ballot secrecy was
eventually broadened to prohibit a member being requested or allowed
to divulge his vote or to assign reasons for his vote on any ballot, as
well as discussions on an unfavorable ballot, this Grand Lodge’s general
rule on ballot secrecy, with a single exception thereto, has remained
substantially the same since 1874.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

159

If Resolution 16-04 is adopted, then this Grand Lodge would create
a second exception to its general rule on ballot secrecy. This second
exception would make it permissible for a discussion of an unfavorable
ballot to take place, and would permit a member to disclose his vote
and the reasons for his vote, only if done in the course of reporting,
preparing, investigating, and/or adjudicating charges of unmasonic
conduct. The resolution does not require a member to disclose his vote
or his reasons for the vote; it permits a member to make such disclosures
if: (1) he chooses to do so; and (2) if done for purposes of reporting,
preparing, investigating and/or adjudicating charges of unmasonic
conduct. Likewise, the resolution does not require that a discussion of
an unfavorable ballot take place and does not make such a discussion
generally permissible; it permits such a discussion only if done in
the course of reporting, preparing, investigating, and/or adjudicating
charges of unmasonic conduct relating to a ballot.
Under CMC Section 1404.010, subsection G(3)(g), the improper use
of ballot constitutes unmasonic conduct sufficient to support the filing
of a charge against a Mason. Yet, an improper use of ballot cannot
presently be proven at trial and unmasonic conduct charges based on
the improper use of the ballot cannot be investigated or adjudicated.
Any Mason willing to testify how he voted in order to prove that the
recorded ballot was incorrect is prohibited from doing so under the
existing language of Section 804.450. For example, if the Master and
Wardens ignored a cube dropped by a brother thereby subverting the
balloting process, charges of unmasonic conduct against the Master and
Wardens could never be proven at trial since the brother that dropped
the cube is prohibited from testifying as to how he voted under the
existing language of Section 804.450. If Resolution 16-04 is adopted, this
problem would be remedied and the ability to investigate and adjudicate
charges of unmasonic conduct relating to a ballot would be expanded by
permitting discussions of unfavorable ballots and permitting a member
to disclose his vote and the reasons for his vote if he chooses to do so.
Report from the Trial Committee
Your Committee on Trial Review offers this report on Resolution 1604. The proponents of this resolution expressly seek to allow a limited
exception to the rule on ballot secrecy when “reporting, preparing,
investigating, and/or adjudicating charges of alleged unmasonic conduct
relating to a ballot.” Currently, the Code mandates that except for the
three officers whose duty it is to examine the ballot box, no one is entitled
to know the number of votes cast for or against an applicant. It further

160

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

provides that there shall be no discussion regarding an unfavorable
ballot. Also, no member of a lodge shall be required, requested, or
allowed to divulge his vote upon a ballot, or to assign reasons for such
vote, if it be known, except to the Master for the purpose of correcting
a mistake.

Resolution No. 16-07
Allows for Alternate Approval of Minutes

Another provision of the Code, however, explicitly provides that
“improper use of ballot” is a ground to support charges of unmasonic
conduct. Improper use of the ballot unfortunately has included acts in
which the officers of the lodge allegedly intentionally failed to accurately
report an unfavorable ballot of the lodge. Under current rules governing
charges of unmasonic conduct, the Committee on Jurisprudence found
that intentional failure to accurately report the result of a ballot was a
sufficient ground to support charges for unmasonic conduct.
Regrettably, due to the restriction and secrecy edict of Section
804.450, the charges could not be proved against the individuals who
purportedly violated the sanctity of the ballot against the will of the
Lodge. Thus, one or more members of the lodge who had cast ballot
against the election of the applicant or for membership by affiliation
whose unfavorable ballots were not properly recorded by the officers
were unable to prove the very violation under the California Masonic
Code. As a result, charges previously filed against one or more officers
of one or more lodges arising from their refusal to properly report the
presence of one or more black cubes were dismissed.
This proposal is not an opening for an unfettered discussion of ballot
results but is expressly limited to the reporting, preparing, investigating,
and/or adjudicating charges of alleged unmasonic conduct relating to a
ballot. This will reconcile the two provisions of the California Masonic
Code and remedy this defect. It will also remove the impunity of the
officers who fail to report the presence of unfavorable ballot without
fear of facing charges of unmasonic conduct for that violation.
For the reasons stated, it the unanimous opinion of the Committee on
Trial Review that the proposed change to Section 804.450 is constructive,
positive and well taken, and therefore recommends a ‘YES’ vote of
Resolution 16-04.
Two members of the Committee being proponents of this Resolution
recused themselves from all deliberations and voting on this report.

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 807.000 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§807.000. STATED MEETINGS.
A lodge shall hold a stated meeting for the transaction of business
once in each calendar month, on the date (other than a Sunday) and
at the time established in its Bylaws. The foregoing notwithstanding,
lodges whose Bylaws provide for meetings fixed by the phase of the
moon shall hold a stated meeting for the transaction of business once
in each lunar month, and Mountain Range Lodge No. 18, Harmony
Lodge No. 164 and Truckee Lodge No. 200 shall only be required to
hold a stated meeting for the transaction of business once in each of 10
calendar months during the year, as it may provide in its Bylaws.
A lodge may be opened for a stated meeting prior to the time fixed in
its Bylaws. However, no business shall be transacted prior to such time.
The Inspector or Grand Master may grant a dispensation to change
the date of a stated meeting, as provided Section 405.060 of this Code.
In the event that the Master of a lodge determines that inclement
weather, including ice, snow, and flood conditions, existing on the day
established in the Bylaws of the lodge for its stated meeting, makes
it hazardous for members of the lodge to attend the meeting, he may,
with the consent of the Inspector of the district to which the lodge is
assigned, postpone the stated meeting to the same day of the week next
following the week scheduled for the stated meeting. The Master shall
notify, to the extent possible, all members of the lodge residing within
50 miles of the meeting place of the lodge of the date of the postponed
stated meeting.
Should a stated meeting be postponed, the business transacted at the
postponed stated meeting shall be limited to approving the reading of
the minutes of the last stated and subsequent Special Meetings, action
thereon, payment of the invoices of the lodge, and such other business of
an important nature as determined by the Master to require immediate
consideration. No other new business shall be considered.

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
Reviewing minutes for accuracy is an important management and
oversight activity. In private business and government, minutes from
previous meetings are often circulated for review. This saves time and
places focus on new issues and tasks. Many lodges have found that
reading their minutes is a lengthy exercise that adds little to their
membership experience. This resolution proposes a solution for those
lodges who would prefer to not read the minutes during their stated
meetings.
This Resolution would amend California Masonic Code Section
805.230—which describes the duties of secretaries—to allow the
Secretary of a lodge to either: (1) read the minutes for approval, as
is current practice; or (2) approve the minutes as distributed so long
as the minutes were made available—with any confidential matters
redacted—at or near the Tiler’s Register at least 60 minutes before
the stated meeting, provided no member requests they be read aloud.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

167

This resolution would also make minor amendments to CMC Sections
807.000 and 807.030 to accommodate this option. It would also authorize
the Committee on Ritual, with the consent of the Grand Master, to make
the appropriate changes in the Monitor and Officer’s Manual.
As CMC Section 804.840 makes clear, the transactions of a Masonic
lodge are not for public consumption. Each Mason has an obligation
to keep his lodge’s transactions confidential. This resolution seeks a
workable balance between this obligation and the desire for shorter
meetings. By requiring the minutes be posted at or near the Tiler’s
Register, a lodge can ensure confidentiality by keeping an attendant
present and collecting all copies before the start of the stated meeting.
By requiring posting for at least 60 minutes before a stated meeting,
members will have ample opportunity to review them, and perhaps,
lead to more effective scrutiny. By allowing any member to require the
minutes be read aloud, each member has an immediate remedy for
any deficiency in the posting. And by requiring confidential portions of
the minutes be omitted from the posted copies, those sensitive matters
not normally read aloud in the reading of the minutes—like Charity
Committee Reports—are also protected from unwarranted disclosure.
If approved, this Resolution would provide lodges a viable option
for shortening their stated meetings, and provide more time on those
activities valued by their membership. However, it would be incumbent
upon each lodge exercising this option to ensure compliance with
CMC Section 804.840 and take precautions to prevent disclosure of the
minutes to non-members.
Resolution: FAILED

It has been the custom of The Grand Lodge of California to not
make changes to ritual, unless there are strong reasons to do so, and

Resolution No. 17-01
Modifies Position of Candidate’s Hands During Third Degree
Obligation
The proponents of this Resolution seek to modify the position of the
candidate’s hands during the third degree obligation so that it more
closely aligns with the current third degree due-guard.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, in ancient times, the position of the candidate’s hands
while taking the third degree obligation was different from that which
is practiced in California today; and
WHEREAS, the due-guard more accurately represents what should
be the position of the candidate’s hands during the third degree
obligation; and
WHEREAS, it is the proponents desire to return the candidate’s
hands during his obligation to the ancient position to conform them to
the current due-guard; and
WHEREAS, as this resolution contains reference to our esoteric
work, any questions about this resolution can be addressed by either
the proponents or members of the Ritual Committee who have been so
advised and are prepared to explain and/or demonstrate the intent of
the esoteric portions of this resolution.

Passage of this resolution would provide clarity and uniformity on a
matter where currently there exists different practices among lodges
and would establish the consensus of this Grand Lodge on hand
placement during the Master Mason obligation.
If adopted, the Inspectors would, under the direction of the Grand
Lecturer and Assistant Grand Lecturers, be in charge of teaching the
proposed hand placement during their schools of instruction.

proceed to work under the revived dispensation, unless legally revoked,
until duly constituted.

the alternative continue the consideration of the petition one time to the
next Annual Communication, in which event the dispensation shall be
revived and the Grand Secretary shall return it, together with the Bylaws,
books of records and returns to the lodge which presented them. The
lodge may then proceed to work under the revived dispensation, unless
legally revoked, until the first day of the next Annual Communication.
Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
The intent of this resolution is to require the Senior Deacon of a lodge
under dispensation or seeking a charter to qualify in the Ritual work
of his office. Currently, the California Masonic Code requires that a
Senior Deacon of a Constituent Lodges must qualify before he can be
installed in his office. There is no similar requirement for a lodge under
dispensation or seeking a charter. While both ceremonies are similar
to an installation of officers of a Constituent Lodge, they are treated
differently under our code.

174

175

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

It has been the policy of the Grand Lodge of California for the Master,
Wardens and Senior Deacon of Constituent Lodges to qualify in the
Ritual Work before they are installed. Since the first CMC was published
in 1931 it has contained sections requiring these qualifications. In
reviewing the proceedings of the Grand Lodge prior to publishing of the
first CMC in 1931 it is clear that these qualifications had been required
for quite some time.

Currently all lodges under dispensation or seeking a charter are
closely monitored by an Inspector assigned by Grand Lodge which
includes making sure that all degree work is performed in accordance
with the CMC. This resolution would add a formal verification of the
qualification of the Senior Deacon before a dispensation or a charter
can be issued. It would require that the Senior Deacon be a member
of the lodge or in the case of a dispensation would join the lodge
if chartered.

It has also been the policy of the Grand Lodge to only require that the
Master and Wardens be qualified in the Ritual of their offices before
a dispensation should be granted by the Grand Master or a Charter
issued by Grand Lodge. There has never been a requirement for the
Senior Deacon to do so.
In 1885, Grand Master Hines made a decision that was approved by
Grand Lodge regarding qualification certificates for only the Master
and Wardens of a newly chartered lodge. A certificate did not need to be
presented at the ceremony if the officers were the same as those listed
on the charter, as the granting of the charter required their qualification,
so it served as the qualification certificate. The decision stated that
this was consistent with long standing policy of Grand Lodge. In 1903
Grand Lodge approved a decision that a lodge under dispensation did
not have to do degree work to get a charter, if the Master and Wardens
were qualified to do the work. This decision appears as a section in the
CMCs published in 1931, 1956 and 1975. It was incorporated into the
section on the requirements for issuing a new charter in the 1991 code.
Both decisions demonstrate that for more than 132 years, Grand Lodge
has maintained separate treatments of the Senior Deacon qualification
for lodges under dispensation or seeking a charter than those of
Constituent Lodges.
It has always been the policy of the Grand Lodge that all work in
this Jurisdiction, including each degree conferred and all lectures, must
be in conformity with the Ritual, and must be adhered to by all lodges
and Masons in this Jurisdiction. The policy of not requiring the Senior
Deacon to qualify in a lodge under dispensation or seeking a charter
does not change that requirement. It allows a lodge under dispensation
or seeking a charter to use any qualified Master Mason to be the Senior
Deacon for degrees, regardless of whether they are a member of the
lodge. The only requirement is that they are qualified to do the work.

The resolution, if passed will require as part of the conditions for a
dispensation or a charter to be granted that a Senior Deacon qualify in
the Ritual work of his office. No qualified Senior Deacon, no dispensation
or charter. The CMC requires all officers of a Constituent Lodge be
installed as soon as is practical after their election or appointment. It
does not mandate which officers have to be installed for a Constituent
Lodge to operate. Therefore, a Constituent Lodge can install its officers
without installing a Senior Deacon. This resolution will place stricter
requirements on lodges under dispensation or seeking a charter than
we place on Constituent Lodges.
If this resolution passes, lodges granted charters during this Annual
Communication will not be affected as it does not take effect until the
close of the session. Lodges currently under dispensation who are
seeking to continue to operate under dispensation after this Annual
Communication will not be affected as they are reviving an existing
dispensation and this resolution applies only to new applications for
dispensations or charters.
Resolution: CARRYOVER

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
The proponents of this resolution wish to add additional officers
to the lodge installation ceremony. California Masonic Code section
805.010 lists the Officers of the lodge. This list is not an all-inclusive list
of officers included in the installation ceremony because the Organist
and Assistant Secretary, for example, are not included in this list. The
CMC also allows for the appointment of other officers that the lodge
may deem appropriate to appoint. But those officers are not currently
part of the installation ceremony.
This resolution calls for the creation and presentation of a jewel of
office for these additional officers. In addition to the jewel, an
accompanying apron must also be provided. These jewels and aprons
must to be approved by the Ritual Committee. Whenever a lodge
wishes to appoint an officer and have them installed to an office that
has not previously been approved, a request must be made to the
Ritual Committee. One lodge may call the officer their Webmaster,
another, their Social Media Officer and yet another, their Community
Communications Officer. All having the same basic duties, but vastly
different titles.

178

179

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

The CMC does not limit the number or types of additional officers that
may be appointed by a lodge, but are not included in the Installation
Ceremony. Where do these officers fall within the jewel march? Where
is their proper place in the lodge? Will the Ritual Committee be
responsible for tracking and consolidating officer titles? This resolution
raises more questions than it answers.

The Grand Lecture and the ritual committee are charged with being
the custodians of our ritual and, through instruction, to maintain its
consistency. It has been the policy of the Ritual Committee to not
recommend changing a practice unless that practice proved, over
the years, to be a burden to the Fraternity in general or to the lodge
in particular. Additionally, the Ritual Committee will support ritual
amendments that allow us to remain relevant and improves the member
experience without jeopardizing our teachings, traditions, and heritage.

It has been the policy of this Grand Lodge to have ritual and
ceremonies as uniform as possible for all Constituent Lodges. This
would change that policy by creating an unknown number of unique
installation ceremonies. For those lodges that wish to avail themselves
of this option, installation ceremonies would take longer. This could
lead to confusion for any brother visiting another lodge.
Report from the Ritual Committee
This resolution seeks to amend the ritual of installation to allow for
the installation of additional appointed officers.
As the proponents point out, the California Masonic Code allows the
lodge Master to appoint additional officers as the lodge may deem proper
to appoint, however, there is no provision in our current installation
ritual for their installation. It should be noted that some current and new
lodges are desirous to appoint, in addition to the required lodge officers,
additional positions such as Director of Ceremonies, Orator, Historian,
Masonic Formation, Almoner, Seat of Fidelity, and Superintendent of
Works, etc.
The adoption of this resolution would have a direct impact upon our
current installation ritual as well as the jewel march.
So what would be the impact upon our Craft if this resolution were to
be adopted? On the one side, it would provide the flexibility for a lodge
to reintroduce into the lodge room forgotten ancient Craft positions as
well as new and innovative positions and offer an opportunity for a
lodge to integrate more members into the lodge officer experience. On
the other side, this resolution could, potentially, introduce an inordinate
number of brethren into the jewel march and introduce inconsistency
in lodge room setup and paraphernalia which could change forever the
traditional face of a number of our lodge rooms in California, however,
with some common sense, this could be avoided.

In the opinion of the ritual committee, this decision should be left to
your collective wisdom.
Should it pass, the adopted verbiage would be modified to allow the
Master to insert a brief description of the officers’ duties as follows:
I.O.
It is your duty to observe the will and pleasure of the
Worshipful Master, to _______________________________________
________________________________ (insert brief description of his
duties) and to perform such other duties as may be required.
You will now repair to your proper place.
The description of the duties would have to be approved by the
Inspector prior to the Installation.
Resolution: FAILED

§809.320. LIFE MEMBERSHIP.
A lodge may adopt a standing resolution providing for a life
membership plan, which shall forever exempt a member making the
required payment into the plan from the payment of dues in the lodge.
The resolution may be adopted, amended or revoked at any stated
meeting by a majority vote of the members present. Any such action
must be presented, in writing, at a preceding stated meeting and written
notice must be given to each lodge member setting forth the text of the
proposed action and the date of the stated meeting at which the vote
is to be taken. The plan must provide that a life membership shall be
granted upon payment of:
A.	A sum of money which is equal to or greater than 17.6 22 times
the lodge’s annual dues at the time of purchase of the life
membership; or
B.	A sum of money equal to the lodge’s annual dues at the time
of purchase of the life membership multiplied by the factor
indicated opposite the member’s age in the following schedule:
Age 49 and under, a factor equal to or greater than 19.2 24
times annual dues;
50 to 54 inclusive, a factor equal to or greater than 16 20 times
annual dues;
55 to 59 inclusive, a factor equal to or greater than 14.4 18
times annual dues;
60 to 64 inclusive, a factor equal to or greater than 12.8 16
times annual dues;
65 to 71 inclusive, a factor equal to or greater than 11.2 14
times annual dues; and
Age 72 and over, a factor equal to or greater than 9.6 12 times
annual dues.

The Secretary shall send to each life member at his last known
address, annually, a life membership Dues Card for the next
calendar year.
A life membership is an executed contract. A life member has no
interest in the lodge’s life membership Fund, except in the case of a
rescission of his life membership with his consent and the consent of
the lodge or as elsewhere provided in this Code.
Upon the rescission of a life membership with the consent of the
lodge and the life member, the life member shall be paid an amount in
cash equal to the lesser of the original sum of money paid to purchase
his life membership or his share of the fair market value of the life
membership Fund at the time of the rescission, as determined by the
Grand Treasurer. In making this determination, the Grand Treasurer
shall compute the interest of each living life member in the lodge’s
life membership Fund and the interest of the lodge in it, on a just and
equitable basis.
The Grand Secretary shall provide the form of contract to be used
by the lodge when a life membership is purchased (other than as a
memorial). Such contract must be signed by the member for whom the
life membership is being purchased, the lodge Master and the lodge
Secretary, affixed with the seal of the lodge. The original shall be kept
as part of the member’s permanent membership record. A copy of the
signed contract shall be provided to the member.
A life member who has been suspended or expelled and who shall
thereafter become restored or elected to membership in a lodge in
which a life membership was once held shall also be restored as a life
member of that lodge.
Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
In April 1850, five lodges sent representatives to Sacramento to form
a Grand Lodge in California. Those representatives determined there
were “the requisite number of duly and constitutionally warranted
lodges to authorize the formation of a Grand Lodge for the State of
California.” They subsequently drafted and adopted the Constitution of
the Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California.

184

185

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Article V of that Constitution gave votes to: each Grand Officer; every
elective Past Grand Officer; three votes to each lodge for its Master and
Wardens, or their representative; and one vote to each lodge for its Past
Masters. This original allocation of votes remains substantially in place
today and is codified in California Masonic Code section 403.075. Thus,
lodges are given equal say at the Annual Communication, provided they
attend and have paid their per capita.

Wardens, Masters, and Past Masters have had the responsibility of
implementing changes to the CMC in their lodges, while most Master
Masons have not.

This resolution would indicate that all members in good standing are
members of Grand Lodge. It should be noted that CMC section 804.115
indicates that one must be a Master Mason to be a member. Thus, this
resolution would make all Master Masons in good standing members of
Grand Lodge and would not make Entered Apprentices or Fellow Crafts
members of Grand Lodge.
This resolution would also give all California Master Masons in good
standing a vote in Grand Lodge. Elected representatives would still be
allowed to cast votes for their absent Masters and Wardens. Also, there
would no longer be a separate Past Master’s vote for each lodge, as each
Past Master would be allowed to vote by virtue of being a Master Mason.
And Master Masons in good standing would be allowed to vote even if
their lodges had not paid per capita.
This is not the first resolution seeking to expand who may vote in
Grand Lodge. Over the last 30 years, there have been 11 resolutions.
Notably, four proposed a vote for each Past Master, one proposed an
increase of each lodge’s Past Master vote from one to four, one proposed
a vote for each lodge Secretary, and one proposed a vote for each
Inspector. The Grand Lodge rejected each of the 11 resolutions.
This Committee identified four major considerations. First, it is unclear
whether this resolution would achieve its stated purpose of increasing
interest and visitation at the Annual Communication. While being able
to vote may provide an incentive to attend Annual Communication, the
deciding factors for attending often revolve around financial capability,
travel distance, family commitments, and work commitments.
Second, while all Master Masons may vote in their lodges, votes in
Grand Lodge have great weight and greater consequence. Just in the
last few years, this Grand Lodge has considered resolutions on cemetery
properties, life membership dues, lodge investments, the reinstatement
of expelled Masons, as well as other topics of statewide importance.

Third, this resolution contains no trial period, or similar method for
retraction, should the resolution be adopted and prove problematic.
Since the number of Master Masons in good standing is substantially
higher than the current number of voting members at Grand Lodge,
if this resolution is adopted, it may not be able to be undone. This is
because revision would require newly enfranchised Master Masons to
voluntarily forfeit their right to vote at Grand Lodge—which is unlikely
to happen.
Fourth, giving a vote to every Master Mason in good standing
would fundamentally change the nature of Grand Lodge. The Grand
Lodge of California was formed 167 years ago by Constituent Lodges.
Its membership consists overwhelmingly of representatives from
Constituent Lodges. Its authority derives from Constituent Lodges. By
giving a vote to every Master Mason, this resolution would transform
the Grand Lodge from an association of Constituent Lodges to an
association of Master Masons. Lodges would no longer be limited to
four votes, rather, lodges would have a vote for every Master Mason
in good standing who attends Annual Communication. A lodge with 60
Master Masons in good standing could have 60 votes; a lodge with 300
could have 300 votes. And lodges located close to San Francisco could
send more voting members at a lower cost than lodges farther away.
This proposed change is within the prerogative of the Grand
Lodge, and it can be rationally seen as either a positive or a negative,
depending upon personal ideology. But as it would be a radical change
from tradition, it deserves careful deliberation.
The Proponents of Resolution 17-05 also seek to reduce the minimum
cost for life memberships by 20%. Section 809.320 of the California
Masonic Code specifies the formula for the cost of a life membership
according to a member’s age.
Historically, in the last 20 years, 14 Resolutions have been presented
on life membership with the majority of those in 2012 and 2013. During
that time only one of those proposals sought to change the cost formula.
Resolution No. 15-03 was carried over to 2016 and then adopted which
increased the cost for all age groups, and amended the groups to include
ages 65 to 71 and age 72 and older.

186

187

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

The Proponents state that a reduction in the cost of life memberships
will provide an incentive to purchase a Life membership. The proposed
rate formula of the Proponents is not only 20% lower than the current
formula but is actually 7-8% less than the formula from 1991, with
the exception of the age group 65-71 which is approximately 2/10
of 1% higher.

WHEREAS, lodges should be able to open in any degree, which
would allow them to continue to be proficient in the ritual of opening
the second and third degrees.

The Committee on Legislative Analysis reported last year that the
previous formula was determined when life expectancy was lower and
conservative investments produced a higher rate of return. The current
rate of return on a 1-year Certificate of Deposit is approximately
1.4%. In 1991 the rate of return on a 1-year Certificate of Deposit was
approximately 6%. Reducing the life membership formula may not
provide a sufficient stream of income to equal the annual dues which
may cause members paying annually to subsidize those in the Life
membership pool.

§402.040. RESTRICTIONS ON CONFERRING DEGREES.

It may be true that a lower priced life membership may produce more
life memberships. However, a life membership that is underpriced is a
financial burden for a lodge.
Resolution: FAILED

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
The intent of this resolution is to allow the presiding officer of a lodge
to conduct business on any degree and to be able to call the lodge up or
down for any purpose.
Prior to the passage of Resolution 11-06 in 2012, stated meetings for
all lodges in California were conducted on the Master Mason degree.
A lodge could not be called up to a higher degree for any purpose
and could be called down to a lower degree only for the purpose
of examination.
Resolution 11-06 changed the California Masonic Code to require all
stated meetings to be held on the Entered Apprentice Degree. Entered
Apprentices and Fellow Crafts were allowed to sit in the stated meeting
but not to vote. Currently, a lodge can be called up to a higher degree or
down to a lower degree only for the purpose of examination.
If adopted, Resolution 17-06 would grant the presiding officer of a
lodge the power to determine on which degree a stated meeting will
be opened. The choice of degree would be at the discretion of the
presiding officer.
This would permit a lodge to open a stated meeting on the third
degree with just five officers and the Tiler instead of seven officers and
the Tiler as required in the first degree opening. It would also allow the
presiding officer to vary the degree opened upon to improve the lodge’s
proficiency in the three different openings.
It would also permit a lodge to conduct Masonic Education on topics
pertaining to the higher degrees at a stated meeting. Currently a
Lodge can only discuss topics pertaining to the first degree at a stated
meeting, since the lodge is only allowed to call up to a higher degree for
examination. This resolution would permit the presiding officer to open
on the first degree for the business portion of the meeting, then calling
up to a higher degree for Masonic Education in the 2nd or third degree,
then calling down to the first degree for closing.
Additionally, there would be no restrictions on the purposes for which
a lodge could be called up or called down. The only requirements are
that degrees and examinations must be conducted in the appropriate
degree and that the lodge be closed on the same degree that it was
opened on. It would be permitted, for example, to open on the first

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

191

degree, call up to the second degree for a Fellow Craft proficiency, call
up to the third degree for a Master Mason conferral, and then call down
to the first degree for closing. It would also be permitted to open on the
third degree, call down to the first degree for conferral of the Entered
Apprentice degree, then call back up to the third degree for closing
(after dismissing the candidate).
This resolution does not require that the presiding officer call down
to a degree that accommodates all Brethren wishing to attend the stated
meeting. It is possible that a presiding officer might choose to always
open on the third degree and not call down to a lower degree for the
business portion of the meeting with the result of excluding all Entered
Apprentices and Fellow Crafts from attending the stated meeting. While
CMC Section 804.860 states that Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts
of the lodge have the right to speak on any matter coming before the
lodge, they do not have the right to require the lodge to operate on a
degree that facilitates their attendance.
If this resolution is adopted, a decision by the Grand Master as to the
restrictions and conditions on the choice of degree by the presiding
officer for conducting a stated meeting may be necessary.
Resolution: CARRYOVER

NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 807.000 of the
California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§807.000. STATED MEETINGS.
A lodge shall hold a stated meeting for the transaction of business
once in each calendar month, on the date (other than a Sunday) and
at the time established in its Bylaws. The foregoing notwithstanding,
lodges whose Bylaws provide for meetings fixed by the phase of the
moon shall hold a stated meeting for the transaction of business once in
each lunar month, and Mountain Range Lodge No. 18, Harmony Lodge
No. 164, and Truckee Lodge No. 200, Big Bear Lodge No. 617 and Rim of
the World Lodge No. 711 shall only be required to hold a stated meeting
for the transaction of business once in each of 10 calendar months
during the year, as it may provide in its Bylaws.
A lodge may be opened for a stated meeting prior to the time fixed in
its Bylaws. However, no business shall be transacted prior to such time.
The Inspector or Grand Master may grant a dispensation to change
the date of a stated meeting, as provided Section 405.060 of this Code.
In the event that the Master of a lodge determines that inclement
weather, including ice, snow, and flood conditions, existing on the day
established in the Bylaws of the lodge for its stated meeting, makes
it hazardous for members of the lodge to attend the meeting, he may,
with the consent of the Inspector of the district to which the lodge is
assigned, postpone the stated meeting to the same day of the week next
following the week scheduled for the stated meeting. The Master shall
notify, to the extent possible, all members of the Lodge residing within
50 miles of the meeting place of the lodge of the date of the postponed
stated meeting.
Should a stated meeting be postponed, the business transacted at the
postponed stated meeting shall be limited to the reading of the minutes
of the last stated and subsequent special meetings, action thereon,
payment of the invoices of the lodge, and such other business of an
important nature as determined by the Master to require immediate
consideration. No other new business shall be considered.

Report from the Legislative Analysis Committee
This resolution seeks to allow Big Bear Lodge No. 617 and
Rim of the World Lodge No. 711 to hold a minimum of ten Stated
Meetings annually.
At the Annual Communication in 2000 this Grand Lodge voted
Mountain Range Lodge No. 18 and Harmony Lodge No. 164 the option
of holding only ten (10) Stated Meetings annually. One year later in
2001, Truckee Lodge No. 200 was given the same option at that year’s
Annual Communication.
Big Bear Lodge and Rim of the World Lodge are located in the
mountains of Southern California. Their problems in the winter are
well explained in the Resolution.
It should be noted that Section 807.000 of the California Masonic
Code provides that the affected Lodge “only be required to hold a Stated
Meeting for ten (10) months of the year.” The approval of this Resolution
will simply add two more Lodges to the exception already in effect in
the CMC.
This resolution balances the importance of holding monthly Stated
Meetings against the ability to safely hold such meetings.

Report of the Board of Trustees
Masonic Homes of California
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
Since 1898, the Masonic Homes has provided relief to our brothers,
their wives, widows, and children in need. This charitable spirit
carries on today through our residential campuses, our communitybased programs through Masonic Outreach Services (MOS), and
The Masonic Center for Youth and Families, providing resources for
distressed children.
In this annual report, I am pleased to share that we are well on
our way towards completing the ambitious goals we defined in our
2015 strategic plan, “Roadmap 2020.” Now halfway through our
journey, we have achieved many important milestones, developing and
implementing impactful programs for members of all ages, supporting
more members in need and creating plans for our future.
As life expectancies rise globally, many elders cannot afford the
basic necessities, let alone the high cost of medical care. We have
approximately 18,300 brothers and widows over age 75. More than 20
percent of Americans over that age live below the poverty level.
MOS is our first point of contact for vulnerable fraternal families,
helping to ensure that our brothers’ wives and widows in need can age
safely and maintain their dignity. Over the past year, we served 356
MOS clients in their communities, close to their lodges and families, the
majority of whom required financial assistance in order to afford basic
necessities and housing. We also created the Masonic Value Network,
designed to help members, conveniently and independently research
and access care in their community.
We continue to reach more members every year. MOS handled more
than 2,000 information and referral calls and made more than 1,000
home visits last year. We expanded the Lodge Outreach Program, which
trains volunteer Masons to lead outreach efforts locally. This important
program extends MOS’ reach while meaningfully engaging members
and reconnecting absent brothers with their lodges.

200

201

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

More than 300 senior Masons and their wives and widows live on our
residential campuses in Union City and Covina. Our residents continue
to thrive, with more than five residents in our 100+ club celebrating
their birthdays this year.

Yet another development in Covina was the opening of the Masonic
Center for Youth and Families’ (MCYAF) Southern Campus location in
December. MCYAF provides family-centered integrated mental health
services to support children and adolescents experiencing emotional,
academic, behavioral, or social difficulties, as well as their families. In
addition to supporting Southern California Masonic families, MCYAF
in Covina has partnered with the Children’s Advocacy Center to serve
children who have been abused witnessed violent crime. We are very
proud of MCYAF’s impact over the past year. The San Francisco center
added educational therapy to its programming and in just a short time,
the Covina and San Francisco centers served 406 clients, a 169 percent
increase from the year before.

After a successful redesign of our wait list, we reduced the time it
takes to move onto one of our Masonic Homes campuses. No longer will
those with the greatest need have to seek other accommodations. I am
pleased to report that we can now provide care on our campus within
three to six months.
Last year’s decision to allow direct admission to the skilled nursing
program has also been a success. Now, more family members in great
need can access the dedicated care they need when they need it.
As Alzheimer’s disease and dementia statistics rise each year,
memory care remains a primary focus. The Stepping Stones program,
which provides successive care strategies to meet the progression of
memory loss, continues to yield positive outcomes. From the Brain
Gym, where residents sharpen memory through neurologist-designed
computer stimulation, to the Compass Club, which has gained national
attention for its innovative approach to daytime care, we are committed
to preserving residents’ cognition as much as possible. We have
demonstrated that memory loss progression can be slowed – and in
some cases, even reversed.
We continue to provide state-of-the-art facilities and best practicefocused care, and are working to expand Southern California resources.
A new health center, offering memory care and skilled nursing will
be opening in Covina by late 2019. This new facility will vastly improve
the quality of life for our elder family members in Covina. As skilled
nursing and memory care are not currently offered there, residents must
be moved to outside accommodations to obtain this care, separating
spouses and causing emotional distress.
We are also pleased to announce that the Covina campus will soon
be home to our first shared housing program. Two of the formerly
unused children’s homes have been remodeled for shared housing,
providing individual privacy within a collaborative, family-like
atmosphere. This innovative approach to senior living will provide
14 seniors with safe housing, where they will benefit from greater
opportunities for socialization, both with fellow housemates and Masonic
Homes residents.

In Union City, we are planning additional capacity to meet the
increasing demand for advanced care, including quality memory care
and high-level assisted living. Our aging buildings are being refreshed
in order to meet this demand, as well as adding additional capacity
through new construction.
All of these programs help us to keep our commitment to you that
we will be here when you need us.
Our greatest resource remains our dedicated professional team,
which continually strives to improve services for the most vulnerable
among our Masonic family and community. This year our leadership
introduced the Masonic Homes Way – a new operating ethos that aims
to create an environment for our residents that stresses efficiency,
experience, personal connection, and safety. Our team’s accomplishments
are recognized beyond our organization. Transitions is consistently
named one of the best short-term, post-surgical rehabilitation programs
in the Tri-City area. The Lorber skilled nursing program maintains a
coveted five-star rating from Medicaid and Medicare – awarded to only
one in 10 such programs nationally. The Union City campus received
a chamber of commerce Green Business of the Year Award for its
reduction in food waste.
We are actively engaged with the Covina and Union City
communities, as well as with brothers statewide. Our newly redesigned
website allows us to share resources across the state more efficiently
than ever. This year, we sponsored several community events
throughout the Tri-City area. SummerFest and HarvestFest brought
nearly 3,000 Masonic family members to our campuses, and MCYAF

hosted a workshop in Union City for adult caregivers – Masons and
non-members. We look forward to welcoming more brothers to our
campuses in the coming year.

july 1, 2016 - june 30, 2017

The Masonic Homes will be here when you need us, and we are
committed to serving you now and in the future. With our reduced
waitlist times, direct-admit skilled nursing program, memory care
resources, statewide outreach programs, and support for youth, our
Masonic family can easily access the quality services they deserve in
their time of greatest need.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Report of the Board of Directors
Acacia Creek Retirement Community

Also, this year Acacia Creek became one of only 19 communities
nationwide to be certified as a Center for Successful Aging. This
certification is awarded to communities that have cultivated a culture
where residents can continue to grow and thrive. This is done through
the leadership’s commitment to assess policies and procedures
and implement change in order to meet the ever-changing needs of
the residents. We do this by providing opportunities in advanced
programming involving the physical, spiritual, social, and intellectual
growth of our residents as the anchor of our Wellness Program.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California
Acacia Creek, our continuing care retirement community, is now
in its seventh year of operation. Financially, Acacia Creek continues to
meet its 25-year pro forma and has begun making payments on the
original bonds.
I am pleased to share with you that Acacia Creek continues to
remain above the national average for occupancy in Independent
CCRC’s across the United States. Our marketing program is focused on
reselling apartments as they become available and expanding our wait
list to quickly identify prospective residents as transitions occur.
Acacia Creek’s success is driven by its current residents’ satisfaction
and happiness, which infuses the campus with a tangible vitality. These
important qualities were evaluated in this year’s Resident Survey, which
indicated Resident Satisfaction at an astounding 97%. Their joyful
spirit is apparent to prospective buyers and visitors, whether they are
joining a resident for a delicious meal, touring the campus, or staying
overnight in one of our well-appointed guest apartments. Acacia Creek
residents demonstrate, through national data collection, that they enjoy
better health, nutrition, and physical activity than those at comparable
communities elsewhere in the country.
In order to continually grow Acacia Creek’s successful aging culture,
the community has partnered with Masterpiece Living. This national
organization provides us with education and programs of physical and
mental wellness inspired by the MacArthur Foundation’s 10-year study
on aging. As a Masterpiece Living community, Acacia Creek residents
are empowered to pursue new skills, physical activities, and personal
fulfillment, as well as contribute to the community by sharing their
skills, knowledge, and life experiences.

Acacia Creek continues to benefit from the camaraderie between
both its Masonic and non-Masonic residents. This year, three more men
became Master Masons since moving in to our community, bringing the
total of non-Masonic residents joining the fraternity to 12; including
the new Administrator, Martin Herter. We hope that many more will
decide to petition in the years to come. Acacia Creek Masons are active
in Siminoff Daylight Lodge at the Masonic Home, and one resident
recently received the Hiram Award for his outstanding service to the
Lodge and Fraternity.
Acacia Creek team members, who follow a team management
concept, report a positive work environment, which is reflected in low
staff turnover. Employees are decision makers who feel a sense of
ownership in the community’s operations. Reliable team members play
a vital role in making the community an ideal place to live.
The fraternity envisioned that Acacia Creek would include all
levels of health care, from independent and assisted living to skilled
nursing and memory care. The Masonic Homes and Acacia Creek
boards continue to collaborate to expand and improve services on
both campuses.
The Acacia Creek community, together, with the Boards of the
Masonic Homes and Acacia Creek are working to further improve the
lives of our current residents with new projects on the horizon.
The Board wishes to extend our sincere appreciation to Chuck
Major, President of Acacia Creek, who has been responsible for the
high level of morale and accountability of the staff and the strategic
Marketing Program that has brought Acacia Creek to stabilization.

218

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

I want to thank the members of the Grand Lodge Executive
Committee, the Grand Lodge staff, the Masonic Homes Board of
Trustees, and the Acacia Creek Board members for their expertise, their
vision, and their passion. We are excited about our future, and together
we look forward to ensuring the continued success and support of the
mission of Acacia Creek.

Report of the Board of Trustees of the
California Masonic Foundation
