To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
The California Masonic Foundation fully embraced its new role in
2017 of overseeing the fundraising for all philanthropic activities within
the jurisdiction. This new role, driven by recommendations from the
Mitchell report of 2015 and by direction of the Executive Committee in
2016, brought about changes to the Board’s structure, membership, and
priorities. In parallel, the Foundation continued to increase the level of
charitable giving by our members, increase our impact on child literacy,
and increase the number of students successfully experiencing our
college access and success programs. Additionally, our Public Schools
Advisory Councils (PSAC) continued to provide local leadership and
fundraising for our literacy and scholarship programs, while the
captains of our Masons 4 Mitts teams enthusiastically raised funds for
baseball gloves for deserving kids. The Foundation also continued to
fund and oversee a variety of impactful programs within and without
the Fraternity.
Fundraising Role
With direction from the Executive Committee in 2016, the
Foundation undertook the added role of being the focal point within
the jurisdiction for all fundraising. Based on recommendations from the
realignment task force, the Foundation began the year by realigning its
structure, adding four new members to the Board with abilities to aid
in fundraising, and creating a three-year fundraising campaign which
was kicked off by the Grand Master during the Annual Communication.
Recognizing the need to meet potential donor expectations, the
Board structure was revised to eliminate the Chief Philanthropy Officer
position on the Grand Lodge staff and replace it with the position of
President of the Foundation. The individual elected to lead the Board of
Trustees was designated Chairman of the Board. The Vice President of
the Board position was eliminated. The ENDS Policy was next revised
to add the responsibility for fundraising. Lastly, with the expansion of
potential Board membership to 21, four new Trustees were added to
the Board:

Child Literacy

The Foundation continued its ongoing relationship with Raising
A Reader (RAR), having now raised more than $1.6M to date and
helping reach 500 classrooms and over 50,000 children. Statistical
data continues to show the impact Raising A Reader has on both
students and their parents by driving parental involvement. During
the year, RAR leadership proposed and the Board approved a joint
effort to expand RAR in California to 1,000 classrooms and to utilize
the Foundation’s ongoing financial commitment as a marketing tool.
In addition, RAR requested $50,000 in new funding to develop a RAR
application for phones/tablets that would help reach more families. The
Board unanimously approved this request.

• Alexander J. Teodoro
• Michael D. Thibodeaux
In addition, representation on the Board by the Masonic Homes of
California was deemed a critical part of the restructure and Michael
Cornell was selected to represent MHC on the Foundation in 2018.
As the year progressed, the President of the Foundation, his staff,
and the VP for Communications defined a major, three-year fundraising
campaign to be known as “Let’s Write the Future.” The campaign was
announced at the Annual Communication with a professional video
highlighting the theme of the campaign. A Steering Committee led by
the Board Chairman was defined to oversee the campaign execution,
and a Chairman of the campaign was created to be the face of the effort.
R. Stephen Doan, PGM agreed to fulfill this role.
In preparation to establish relationships with the members and
lodges who will make this campaign a success, two sub-committees
were created to focus on these activities and work with Foundation staff.
The first committee will focus on lodge relations and donations and was
divided into north and south groups, with Robert Whitfield chairing the
north and Randy Brill chairing the south. The second committee will
primarily focus on individual relationships and donations.
Public School Advisory Councils (PSAC)
Once again, our eight PSACs were our boots on the ground and
did outstanding work in coordinating successful Public Schools
Month Kick Off events in seven areas of the state. Attendance by
the brethren increased and more than $900,000 was given to school
districts representing the money invested by the Masons of California
in literacy programs and college success scholarships in their area. The
PSACs helped raise these funds by traveling to lodges to inform them
of the Foundation’s work and solicit donations. They also interview the
potential Investment in Success scholarship candidates from their area.
The Board of Trustees is extremely grateful for the dedicated efforts of
these brothers.

Investment in Success
This year our PSACs interviewed candidates identified by our
college access and success partner organizations and recommended
awarding scholarships to 93 deserving students. This brings the
number of students in the program to more than 300. Over $600,000 in
scholarships was distributed this year. In addition, our success partners
continue to follow our students through their academic endeavors,
providing aid, advisors, and specialized support services to increase the
probability of graduation and a successful life.
The Foundation also granted new Masonic Youth Leadership
Scholarships to 23 members of our youth orders, worth $69,000. We
are proud to be able to support the continuing education of these fine
youth leaders.
Teacher of the Year
The Foundation continued its commitment as a leading supporter
of the California Teacher of the Year program for the 23rd year. At the
annual ceremony held in Sacramento in February, the Grand Master
handed out checks to the five finalists as well as the semi-finalists.
The Superintendent of Education once again publicly highlighted the
support of the Masons of California. The finalists also received gifts
from the Foundation at the celebration events in their own districts.

Masons4Mitts (M4M)
The successful Masons 4 Mitts program continued into its eighth
year supporting the foundations of the SF Giants, LA Dodgers and SD
Padres with funds to purchase baseball gloves for deserving youth.
The M4M teams competed to raise the most money, which continues

was raised this year and checks were presented during Masons’ Night
at AT&T Park, Dodger Stadium, and Petco Park. In addition, the LA
Angels organization agreed to become part of the program and teams
will raise funds for them beginning in 2018. To show our appreciation,
160 Masons attended a game at Angels Stadium.

The Board is entrusted with the preservation, maintenance, and
future viability of the landmark California Masonic Memorial Temple
building that inspires and serves our members.
This year, CMMT marks its 59th year located at 1111 California
Street in San Francisco. Since its opening, it has served as a location
for Masonic gatherings, and as a venue for concerts and other cultural
events enjoyed by the greater community.
The California Masonic Memorial Temple is proud to report another
very successful year. CMMT operations continue to be strong and
predictable. Live Nation remains a good tenant and partner, producing
high quality concerts and corporate events.
Financial performance has been strong and predictable. Positive
cash flow for the year is forecasted to be more than $400,000 - up
significantly from last year.
We are in the process of planning further into the future and have
contracted for a professional survey of the building and its systems to
provide a 10-year capital plan. Our five- and 10-year plans will address
ways to create greater efficiency and reduce expenses in the operation
of the building, particularly as it relates to utility expenses. To help
reduce energy costs and contribute to a greener community, a solar
system has been installed in conjunction with Nob Hill and additional
roof enhancements were included in the project. We also completed
the replacement of some of the exterior doors and a few interior doors.
We are exploring renovations that would allow for increased
Masonic use of the building throughout the year.
Our neighborhood relations continue to be very good. CMMT is a
strong supporter of the neighborhood and holds quarterly meetings
through the Nob Hill Community Liaison Group. Our Executive Vice
President ,Allan Casalou, continues to serve as a director for the
Nob Hill Association as well as on its Park Committee and Security
Committee. On October 11 we hosted one of the Nob Hill Associations
monthly events and exhibited a celebration of the 300th Anniversary of
Freemasonry. Our neighbors toured the auditorium which was set up for
the Annual Communication and shared some of our best archives with

We hope that the brethren will make it a point to visit the California
Masonic Memorial Temple on Nob Hill when in San Francisco and
take advantage of the collections of the Henry Wilson Coil Library and
Museum, view the endomosaic mural designed and constructed by
Emile Norman and attend the variety of concerts held in the auditorium.
The Board wishes to extend its appreciation to Julia Gordon in
preparing and managing our meeting materials and schedule, our
Executive Vice President and Grand Secretary Allan Casalou, our Chief
Financial Officer Thomas J. Boyer, Director of Financial Planning Khalil
Sweidy, Treasurer Arthur Salazar, and especially the staff who work
so diligently to represent our interests and to maintain and manage
the building. We also thank the Grand Master, Most Worshipful John
Heisner, for the opportunity to serve and for his active support and faith
in our efforts.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California, F. & A.M.,
The Board of Directors for the NHMC are pleased to present this
annual report to the Grand Lodge of California and its members.
As the Grand Lodge’s only for-profit entity, our Primary End’s Policy
is to ensure that the garage at the California Grand Lodge Masonic
Temple on Nob Hill in San Francisco operates efficiently and effectively
in order to generate an annual profit to pay Grand Lodge of California,
its stockholder, an annual dividend. This dividend provides the Grand
Lodge essential funding for ongoing operational activities.
Each year your board and executive team continue to explore new
and alternative resources to keep the garage operations profitable. Our
executive team, led by Very Worshipful Allan Casalou and our Chief
Financial Officer, Tom Boyer, has continued its excellent work toward
achieving our financial goals by seeking out new professional garage
management and continuing the process of converting our energy
source over to a new solar system.
This year brought an end to the Ace Parking management contract.
In preparation for this, the team sent out several Request for Proposals
(RFPs) to a select group of parking lot operators. After review of
the proposals, Ace and SP Plus were determined the two finalists.
While Ace was the incumbent manager and has managed the garage
well, they did not deliver the additional revenue sources that they
had originally proposed. SP Plus is a larger, national company with
many more resources at its disposal. They employ their own internal
marketing team, link to many online parking apps and websites, and
bring to the operations several very experienced garage managers. We
believe that with SP Plus’s increased and focused bandwidth, parking
revenue will increase. Our garage will be listed on several parking apps
and websites; so while customers and visitors to Nob Hill are searching
for events and activities, our parking garage will pop up as an available
parking provider, and offer a means of pre-paying and reserving a
parking space ahead of time. This is a key element in the success of our
garage as convenience of finding venues and parking is done online
and through device applications, the NHMC garage will be advertised

Additionally this year, we commenced and completed the conversion
of our garage power source to solar power. Solar panels are now installed
on the roof of our Grand Lodge. With the installation of the solar panels,
we evaluated to condition of the roof, addressed the roof needs, and
prepared it for installation of the new panels. A major improvement,
this power conversion will provide large energy savings for our
operations as well as significant tax savings – all of which help to lower
our bottom line. These savings are in addition to previous cost saving
measures implemented last year when the garage automation system
was upgraded and lights in the garage were converted from fluorescent
to LED lighting. We are thankful for Tom Boyer’s management of these
cost-saving efforts.
Overall business and hospitality on Nob Hill has decreased over
the last year. Hotels report vacancy rates are higher than normal as a
result of less SF convention activity due to the temporary closure of the
Moscone Convention Center while it is under renovation. Several Bay
Area mainstay businesses who usually conduct their conventions and
conferences here is San Francisco have relocated their events to the
South Bay. There has also been a dip in large and small events on Nob
Hill and at the NHMC. This drop in business has translated into less
parking revenue than projected in our budget. On the flip side, since
there is less business, expenses to run the garage are also down.
Fortunately, the executive team’s efforts to manage expenses and
control costs has enabled the NHMC to continue to provide a modern
and safe parking venue for visitors. The combined cost measure savings
of parking automation plus lower energy use/cost measures such as
light bulb replacement, solar panel tax credits, and lower solar energy
costs will generate yet another profitable year. Last year, NHMC was
proud to deliver the largest dividend to Grand Lodge in history. Once
again, NHMC is proud to announce that we will pay Grand Lodge

Report of the Committee
on Jurisprudence
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Committee on Jurisprudence serves as the legal adviser to the
Grand Master and the legal adviser to the Grand Lodge when in session.
The committee reviews proposed resolutions and recommendations
to be considered at the next Annual Communication and prepares
any necessary legislation to carry out the intent of the proponents.
At the Annual Communication, it comments on the legality of the
Grand Master’s decisions and dispensations and on the legal effect
of the proposed recommendations and resolutions. After the Annual
Communication, it prepares the changes to the California Masonic Code
to reflect the legislation that was adopted.
In the committee’s view, those of Grand Master Heisner’s decisions
and dispensations coming to its attention were legal and within his
discretion. In the committee’s view, the legislation posted by the Grand
Secretary to the Grand Lodge website on July 10 of this year is sufficient
to carry out the intent of the proponents. We believe that each piece of
this legislation has the legal effect set forth in it.
In presenting the legislation for your consideration, we make no
recommendations as to the action you should take with it. While the
committee has written the title and introductory explanation for each
resolution before you and assisted the proponents in drafting the Code
changes required to affect their intent, the proponents’ arguments in
their whereas clauses are their own. The committee does not assist in
drafting the whereas clauses and makes no comments on them.
The legislation posted by the Grand Secretary to the Grand Lodge
website on July 10 of this year requires no separate motion because it is
automatically before this Annual Communication. The presiding officer
will announce the vote required for the passage of each item before
discussion begins. Any legislation that does not amend the California
Masonic Code or the Ritual requires a simple majority only for adoption.
Any amendment to the California Masonic Code or the Ritual must be
adopted by a five-sixths affirmative vote. If the amendment receives a
simple majority but less than a five-sixths affirmative vote, it carries over
to the next Annual Communication when only a two-thirds affirmative
vote is required for adoption.

In addition to the foregoing responsibilities, the committee reviews
all charges and specifications of unmasonic conduct, strikes out those
portions which are not supported by a clear and precise specification
of unmasonic conduct and revises those portions which are incorrect,
ambiguous or insufficient. The committee may dismiss charges if all of
the facts set forth in the specifications, even if true, would not warrant
a verdict of unmasonic conduct. As part of its review, the committee
provides the parties with every essential factual element which must be
proven at trial in order for the Accused to be found guilty of each charge.
Since the last Annual Communication, the committee has reviewed the
charges and specifications in twenty-two trials.

Exhibit
Automatic Expulsions
October 30, 2016 to October 12, 2017

If a Mason under the disciplinary jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge
has pleaded guilty or nolo contendere (or no contest) to, or has been
convicted of, a crime of moral turpitude by a federal or state court, he
shall be deemed automatically expelled from all the rights and privileges
of Masonry without any further action of his Lodge or Grand Lodge.
The committee reviews a certified copy of the record of conviction to
determine whether there has been an automatic expulsion. Since the
last Annual Communication, the committee has reviewed six federal
or state court records to evaluate whether there has been an automatic
expulsion of the Mason involved in the proceeding. These matters are
summarized in the attached exhibit.
We thank the Grand Master for the opportunity which he has given
us to serve this year.

Trial No. 2730
In Trial No. 2730, the member pled no contest to a violation of
California Penal Code Section 288.4(b). Under Section 100.075 of
the California Masonic Code and 2009 Grand Master’s Decision No.
2, an attempt to commit a lewd act involves moral turpitude. In the
Committee’s opinion, the conduct described in California Penal Code
Section 288.4(b) involves an attempt to commit a lewd act. Therefore, the
member was automatically expelled from all the rights and privileges of
Masonry pursuant to Section 1404.820 of the California Masonic Code.
His expulsion from Masonry was effective on September 4, 2014, the
date he entered his plea of no contest.
Trial No. 2791
In Trial No. 2791, the member pled no contest to a violation of
California Penal Code Sections 182 and 487, before he became a
Mason. Under Section 100.075 of the California Masonic Code and 2009
Grand Master’s Decision No. 2, a conspiracy to commit theft involves
moral turpitude. In the Committee’s opinion, the conduct described in
California Penal Code Sections 182 and 487 involves a conspiracy to
commit theft. Therefore, the member was automatically expelled from
all the rights and privileges of Masonry pursuant to Section 1404.820 of
the California Masonic Code. His expulsion from Masonry was effective
on September 20, 2012, the date he became a Mason.
Trial No. 2802
In Trial No. 2802, the member pled guilty to a violation of 18 U.S.C.
Section 201(c)(1)(B). Under Section 100.075 of the California Masonic
Code and 2009 Grand Master’s Decision No. 2, bribery involves moral
turpitude. In the Committee’s opinion, the conduct described in 18
U.S.C. Section 201(c)(1)(B) involves bribery. Therefore, the member was
automatically expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry
pursuant to Section 1404.820 of the California Masonic Code. His
expulsion from Masonry was effective no later than February 10, 2016,
the date of the court document on which the Committee has relied.

Report of the Committee on Insurance
Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & .M. of California,
The Insurance Committee is tasked with the responsibility of
reviewing the Grand Lodge property, casualty, professional lines
insurance policies, and other related insurance programs; working with
the broker selected by Grand Lodge and making recommendations
regarding coverage and other insurance related matters. The Insurance
Committee reports to the Grand Secretary on all insurance matters
(except life and medical coverage and benefits for employees), who
then makes the final decision regarding the different coverages and
limits to purchase or renew. The committee also works closely with the
Chief Financial Officer and Legal on an ongoing basis.
Currently there are three meetings a Masonic year of the full
Committee and an additional meeting in December for just the
Chairman, Vice Chairman, the CFO, other Grand Lodge representatives,
and the Insurance Broker.
The purpose of this meeting is to advise the broker of any changes
to Grand Lodge activities or exposures to loss as well as review new
programs being contemplated or under way. The broker provides
any information on changes in the insurance market place regarding
cost, coverage, and availability. The broker may also make new
recommendations regarding the insurance program.

2016-17 Grand Lodge Insurance overview
Last year we reported a stronger relationship with our broker Marsh.
Moving forward, this year Marsh has continued to prove themselves
good partners and their team understands our needs and expectations.
All parts of the insurance program were successfully renewed
effective April 1, 2017 with some special notations as follows:
a.

The Property All Risks policy saw an increase in total values
but still had an overall 9.8% decrease in premium. The coverage
for terrorism was broken out from this policy which accounts
for almost half the premium savings.

b.

Property All Risks – Terrorism. Stand-alone terrorism coverage
was purchased at a competitive rate not available within the
Property All Risks policy thereby accessing an additional 8%
premium savings.

c.

DIC/EQ policy had a 10% premium decease (not including Halls
and MCYF ).

d.

Commercial General Liability increased 1.3% over last year’s
flat renewal. This is an increase in premium of $4,200.

e.

Auto Liability renewed with a 4% premium increase due to the
addition of one unit.

f.

Workers Compensation; the deductible policy estimated
premium increased by 2.65% (payroll increased by 6.22%). The
guaranteed program has an estimated premium increase of
7.34% (payroll increased by 6.41%).

g.

$25M umbrella liability policy was renewed with a premium
increase over last year of less than 1%.

Report of the Investment Committee
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Overview
The Investment Committee has been charged with the prudent
handling of Grand Lodge investment funds. These funds consist
primarily of the General and Endowment funds for the Masonic Homes
of California, but also include the investment portfolios of the California
Masonic Foundation, California Masonic Memorial Temple, the Grand
Lodge Retirement plan and the Grand Lodge itself. We take this charge
very seriously. In its simplest terms, we manage the investment funds
with an eye to grow and preserve capital. We strive to maintain an
increasingly diversified portfolio that is designed to generate the
necessary funds for the continuing operation of Masonic functions as
well as to allow for growth for future needs. In doing so, we constantly
scan the horizon in an attempt to manage the funds to take advantage of
long-term trends as well as near-term opportunities. The Grand Lodge
Investment Committee utilizes the services of professional investment
management firms to gain access to the capital markets. The funds are
invested in the domestic United States, international equity markets,
fixed income markets, and alternative strategies which are not as
correlated to the traditional stock and bond markets.
The past year (ending June 30th, 2017) yielded a return of 14.1% on
the invested funds. We recognize that not all years can be positive years,
and we remain committed to the process and to the structure of the
portfolio as constructed. We have spent a good deal of time finding ways
to balance risk and reward in the portfolio. We have spent a great deal
of our time analyzing the strategic allocation to various asset classes
in the portfolio with the help of our new consultants (NEPC, LLC). We
implement a mix of traditional equity investments, as well as fixed
income and alternatives. A primary driver of the allocation strategy
is to assemble a collection of investments that do not share a direct
correlation in risk profile (so all the assets do not react the same to
down market conditions).

240

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge & Related Entity Investment Performance For the
year ended June 30th, 2017
The Total Grand Lodge and Related Entities portfolio grew 14.1% for
the year ending June 30, 2017. The total fund policy benchmark was up
12.3% and the Consumer Price Index for the year was 1.0%. The market
value of the Total Grand Lodge and Related Entities portfolio as of June
30, 2017, was $1,021,627 compared to $846,636,983 a year earlier. For
the three-year period ending June 30, 2017, the combined Grand Lodge
and related entities returned 4.3% versus 5.8% for the benchmark. Since
inception, our funds have returned 7.7% annually versus 7.8% return of
the benchmark.
The U.S. equity allocation of the portfolio was up 21.4% compared to
+18.5% for the Dow Jones Total Stock Market Index. The Non-U.S. equity
portfolio was up 19.9% compared to 20.5% for the MSCI All Country
World ex-U.S. Index. Global Equities were up 22.7% compared to 18.8%
for the MSCI All-Country World Index. The fixed income portfolio
was up 1.4%, compared to a -2.2% return for the Fixed Income Custom
Benchmark. Our Total Hedge Funds and GAA Hedge Funds were up
7.1% compared to the HFRI Fund Weighted Index of 6.2%. And our Total
Private Markets were up 9.0%. A more detailed manager performance
review can be found in the tables following this report.
The Investment Committee does not attempt to take advantage of
perceived short-term anomalies in the markets by chasing the most
recent top performing asset class. Rather, it arrives at its recommended
allocation to stocks and bonds and other asset classes only after very
careful due diligence and consideration. The purpose of the funds, their
spending requirements, investment time horizon and ability to assume
risk are all factored into these recommendations. The probability and
duration of potential losses are carefully weighed against the long-term
potential for appreciation of assets after withdrawals are taken into
account. The Investment Committee recommends asset allocations that
will provide the highest probability that the funds will be able to meet
their respective objectives over the long-term.
All returns are net of fees. Detailed Entity performance can be
found in the tables following this report.

241

Summary of Recent Changes
This year, several changes were made to the overall portfolio
structure, which necessitated changes to the Investment Policy
Statement (IPS). Per the CMC, the Masonic entity boards approved
these changes and the highlights are summarized below.
The major revisions to the Statement are:
• Governance changes. Sections 5 and 6, which had specified that
the committee will conduct on-site due investment manager
diligence, were deleted in order to give the committee greater
hiring flexibility.
• Fund Objectives/Relevant Market Indices. A total return goal for
the portfolio used by the committee was explicitly incorporated
into the statement and benchmark indices were updated
or changed as a result of changes to asset allocation targets
noted below.
• Investment Allocations. While the general asset classes set out
in the Statement remain essentially unchanged, equity asset
allocations were reduced and alternatives asset allocations
were increased. In particular, maximum equity allocation was
reduced from 65% to 60% and target equity allocation was
reduced from 55% to 50%. Target and maximum alternatives
allocations were increased from 30% and 35%, respectively, to
35% and 45%. (See pages 12 and 13.) The Alternatives asset
category was also broken out in the revised Statement into subcategories: Total Hedge Funds and Global Assets Allocation,
and Private Markets.
• These allocation changes were subjected to liquidity and
stress testing to ensure that the re-balanced portfolio could be
expected to perform in a manner consistent with MHC’s and
Acacia Creek’s bond financial covenants.
• Investment Manager Changes. Within the asset categories, the
committee elected to make significant changes with respect to
the selection of particular investment managers.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge Investment Management For the year ended
June 30th, 2017
In order to fulfill our responsibilities in accordance with the Grand
Lodge Investment Policy and Philosophy, the Investment Committee
meets quarterly with our Investment Consultant, NEPC, LLC. We also
meet with our individual portfolio managers as needed and review due
diligence reports quarterly from the consultants. We monitor respective
performance of the managers compared to various indices representing
their objective. This process provides the Investment Committee with
the necessary data to evaluate each investment manager on a timely
basis, and to observe whether they continue to achieve the objectives
of their mandate.
The committee also holds monthly conference calls (as needed)
to discuss any outstanding business, or discuss the implementation of
tactical changes within the portfolio.
Finally, we have scheduled bi-annual retreats to take time to review
our overall strategic initiatives implemented over the prior two years,
review the macro environment and opportunities therein and chart a
course for the following two-year period.
Our Investment Consultant, “NEPC, LLC,” is a new relationship that
began in January 2017. We are happy to report that the relationship
is going well and we very much appreciate the “deep dive” that this
new consultant has helped us perform on the overall allocation and
assignment to managers.
Your Grand Lodge Investment Committee is also available to assist
individual lodges in determining appropriate investment strategy.
One available vehicle to aid in this effort is the “Lodge Investment
Options Program” which is intended to assist lodges in determining
an appropriate investment strategy and asset allocation. Whether you
currently have lodge investments or are considering implementing
such a program, we direct your lodge trustees’ or investment committee
members’ attention to the Member Center website for more information
on this turnkey program. We are also here to help lodges establish a
set of policies and procedures that are designed to ensure assets are
invested according to the needs of the lodge and to safeguard against
the misuse of funds. Investment Committee members continue to make
themselves available to the lodges for assistance with this program and
other questions regarding lodge investments.

Report of the Committee on Lodge Support

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California,

The 2016-17 Grand Lodge year found the Lodge Support Committee
(LSC) engage with 26 lodges. Approximately six required minor
interactions and or resources; we rehabilitated three with an additional
three considering consolidation and unfortunately a few suspensions
as well. The remaining lodges are works in progress with hopes that all
will show improvement in the near future.

This year the Lodge Support Committee (LSC) underwent
significant adjustments by leveraging our AGL’s and Inspectors as
local resources in response to lodges and their needs. Our desire
is to have lodges think of the LSC more of a “Lodge Coach” than a
troubleshooter. This approach was exemplified during our retreat
weekends for lodge officers. Consequently, we were fortunate enough
to have numerous workshops at each of the retreats providing elective
sessions for attendee’s to participate in best practice discussion on the
specific issues they are currently addressing. More than 90 current
officers availed themselves of these late night workshops and provided
valuable feedback on its efficacy and value. During these workshops,
we informed the attendees of the numerous resources available on the
LSC webpage’s and previewed the arrival of our upcoming surveys.
As promised we now have a series of 11 surveys available on our
website to enhance the member experience and enable each lodge to
align its deliverables with member expectations. These surveys are for
lodges to poll their membership in the following areas:

252

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Lodge evaluation serves as one of the most important areas, whereby
each lodge can get a report card from its membership on how they did
that year based upon 17 criteria from advertising to Ritual, budgeting to
social media, and community service to Youth Order involvement.

Report of the Committee on Trial Review

253

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California,

Our main focus in addition to helping lodges become more
responsive to their membership is also providing lodges with as many
resources as possible to achieve their goals.

The Committee on Trial Review has carefully examined the records
of all trials completed during this Masonic year. All committee votes
were unanimous except where otherwise noted.

My sincere appreciation goes to all of my committee members
who worked so arduously during the year and to my Vice Chair, Shawn
Donahue, for his tireless efforts and dedication to our Fraternity.

In each of the following matters, the committee finds that there was
compliance with the procedural requirements of the California Masonic
Code, and that the findings were supported by substantial evidence
except where otherwise noted.

Fraternally,
Gary C. Silverman, Chairman

The following cases were decided by the Trial Masters after
investigation either because the Accused failed to submit a plea under
California Masonic Code section 1404.410, or submitted a plea of guilty
or no contest under section 1404.420.

Antonio G. Cimarra Jr.
Charles P. Cross
Ricky L. Lawler
Gary R. Quintrell
Matthew W. Ross

Thomas E. Colgan
David M. Edwards
Elvan D. Moen
Victor M. Ropac Jr.
Jeffery M. Wilkins

1. In Trial Number 2773, the Accused, an attorney, was arrested,
charged and convicted of a felony under California Penal Code
Section 4573(A) for smuggling 36.09 grams of heroin worth
approximately $30,000 intended for his client awaiting trial
for murder in the Los Angeles County jail. The State Bar of
California had disbarred the Accused for moral turpitude as a
result of the conviction. The Trial Master found that the Accused
actions involved moral turpitude and constituted unmasonic
conduct and fixed the penalty at expulsion. One member
recused himself and did not participate in the discussion or
voting. The remaining members of the committee agreed with
the procedures, the findings, and penalty.
2. In Trial Number 2775, the Accused, the Treasurer of the Hall
Association, was accused of embezzlement. The Accused linked
his personal bank account with that of the Hall Association
maintained at the same bank. The Accused then made online
unauthorized withdrawals in the sum of $8,000.00 from the Hall’s
bank account.When confronted, the Accused denied having linked
his personal account with the Hall’s bank account. However, a
subsequent inquiry disclosed that the bank’s policy did not allow
for such a link between unrelated personal and business accounts
without a request by the customer. Additionally, the evidence
demonstrated that he tried to borrow funds to “repay” the Hall

254

Proceedings of the

Association and admitted to having “inadvertently transferred
the money to his account.” The Trial Master determined that the
Accused had been in financial distress for a period of time prior to
the transfers from the Hall Association’s account to his personal
account. The Trial Master found that the conduct was unmasonic
involving moral turpitude and fixed the penalty at expulsion. The
committee agrees with the Trial Master’s procedures, findings,
and the penalty.
3. In Trial Number 2782, the Accused was charged with embezzling
$279,651.00 from the Lodge from 2012 through 2014 while he was
serving as its Treasurer. The embezzlement was discovered during
an audit in 2016 after the Accused had failed to make the required
financial disclosures and reports for four years. The Trial Master
made numerous attempts to contact the Accused and allow him
to answer the charges including sending three separate certified
letters, personally visiting three addresses listed in Grand Lodge
and other records, placing numerous telephone calls, and sending
at least one email. Having not received a response, the Trial Master
performed his investigation in accordance with the California
Masonic Code and found that the specifications for the charges
were supported by the evidence and that the Accused’s actions
involved moral turpitude and accordingly were unmasonic. He
affixed the penalty at expulsion. The committee agrees with the
Trial Master’s procedures, findings and penalty.
4. In Trial Number 2785, the Accused was charged with embezzling
funds from the Lodge from June 2015 through 2016. The
embezzlements included: (1) receiving cash for deposit in the
lodge account but failing to do so; (2) using the lodge ATM card
to make unauthorized withdrawals from the lodge account;
(3) cashing a lodge check in the amount of $650 to attend the
Secretary and Treasurer’s Retreat but failing to pay the same to
Grand Lodge. Initially the Accused pled “not guilty as to lack of
intent” to the charges, but then changed his plea to “No Contest.”
A Lodge Audit confirmed the embezzlement in the total amount
of $4,571 covering 20 transactions. The Trial Master found the
conduct to be unmasonic involving moral turpitude and imposed
the penalty of expulsion. The committee agrees with the Trial
Master’s procedures, findings, and penalty.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

255

The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for the
adoption of the following Resolution: “Resolved, that in Trial Numbers
2773, 2775, 2782 and 2785, the Trial Masters’ procedures, findings and
the penalties affixed be hereby affirmed.”
5. In Trial Number 2787, the Accused, a sitting Master, was charged
with five specifications which revolved around balloting for
membership by affiliation. The charges included that the Accused
allowed open discussion of the results of an unfavorable ballot
in violation of section 804.450 of the California Masonic Code;
improperly declared the results of the ballot void, rescheduled
re-balloting in the next stated meeting, and improper handling of
the ballot box including the alleged removal of black cubes. The
Accused submitted a brief in support of his defense in which he
claimed he “nullified the ballot and re-balloted the applications.”
The Accused pled guilty to specification number one of nullifying the
ballot and rescheduling balloting, the Commissioners found him guilty
and imposed the penalty of reprimand, the remaining specifications
were dismissed, to which the committee agrees.
The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves
for the adoption of the following Resolution: “Resolved, that in Trial
Number 2787, the Commissioners procedures, findings and the penalty
affixed be hereby affirmed.”  
6. 
In Trial Number 2790, the Accused was charged with two
specifications arising from social media postings in which he
reproduced in English portions of the esoteric work, disparaged
his lodge and various members, and referred to a brother in a
derogatory and threatening manner. The Trial Master found him
guilty of the specifications and found the act unmasonic. The
Trial Master affixed the punishment at reprimand on one of the
charges and suspension of 12 months for the second charge.
Our Code does not recognize double or multiple penalties on
different specifications. This is not only fair, but also avoids the practical
problems associated with disparate punishments. The Committee
recommends that the penalty be changed to 12 months suspension and
that the penalty of reprimand be stricken.

The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for the
adoption of the following Resolution: “Resolved, that in Trial Number
2790, the Trial Master’s procedures and findings be affixed, but that the
penalty be affixed at a suspension of 12 months and that the penalty of
reprimand be stricken.”

The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for the
adoption of the following Resolution: “Resolved, that in Trial Numbers
2783 and 2784 the Trial Master and Commissioners’ procedures, findings
and verdict be hereby affirmed.”

The following trials were conducted with testimony taken.
7. In Trial Number 2778, the Accused was charged for intentionally
striking the Accuser in the face in violation of California Masonic
Code section 1401.010.G.2.c proscribing personal violence on
a Mason. The Trial Master found that based on the evidence
presented at trial the Accused struck Accuser and that the act
was unmasonic. The Trial Master declared that the evidence
did not support an intent to cause great bodily harm and that
the altercation did not escalate beyond the initial touching.
The Accused also in his testimony disclosed that he felt he was
in danger during the scuffle and was also struck, though this
was unclear to the Trial Master, when and by whom the assault
occurred, even though the Accused pointed to the Accuser and
another individual as the culprits. Based on the evidence at trial,
the Trial Master affixed the penalty at a definite suspension of
six (6) months. The committee agrees with the decision of the
Trial Master and recommends its approval.
The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for the
adoption of the following Resolution: “Resolved, that in Trial Number
2778 the Trial Master’s procedures, findings and penalty affixed be
hereby affirmed.”
8. Trial Numbers 2783 and 2784 is a consolidated matter involving
two Accused and was tried before a Trial Master and
Commissioners. Of the four specifications, three related to the
rental of the Hall Association for a private party and the fourth
charge related to the alleged refusal of both Accused to obey the
authority of the Master properly exercised of excluding them
from a stated meeting.
The Trial Master and the Commissioners unanimously found that
the evidence did not support the four specifications of unmasonic
conduct and that the Accuser had failed to meet his burden of
proof to demonstrate unmasonic conduct. The Committee agrees
with the decision of the Trial Master and Commissioners and
recommends its approval.

The Trial Masters dismissed the following matters.
9. In Trial Number 2711, the Accused was charged with specifications
arising from a business owned by the Accused and invested in by
the Accusers. Additionally, the Accusers were employees of one of
the businesses. The charges included a failure to pay them payroll
resulting in the filing of a claim with the Labor Commissioner.
While the Labor claim was pending, the Accused filed personal
bankruptcy and his two businesses also filed for bankruptcy. The
second charge concerned certain alleged false representations
made by Accused to the Accuser between May 2009 to April 2011.
The final charge is that Accused sold three rifles of Accuser and
failed to give the proceeds of the sale to the Accuser.
During the time the charges were pending the Trial Master
replaced the original Accuser for failure to diligently prosecute
the charges. The new Accuser was unable to communicate with
the aggrieved brethren despite various efforts. He also was
unable to obtain the file from the prior Accuser despite various
requests. Accordingly, he filed a motion to dismiss the charges.
The Trial Master accepted the motion and accordingly dismissed
the charges. Two members of the committee recused themselves
from the discussion and voting on the review. The remaining
members of the committee unanimously affirmed the Trial
Master’s dismissal of the charges.
The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for the
adoption of the following Resolution: “Resolved, that in Trial Numbers
2711, the Trial Master’s dismissal of the charges is affirmed.”
10. Trial Numbers 2768 and 2771 were consolidated for Trial as the
Accuser for both cases is the same and both matters related
to the same subject matter and transactions. The Accused in
matter number 2768 was charged with three specifications: (1)
for falsehood, treachery and deceit in that the Accused took
sides against a brother during divorce proceedings; (2) misled
the court with regard to various representations before the

258

Proceedings of the

court; (3) made loans to the member’s former spouse; and (4)
assisted with advertising for the former spouse in local Shrine
publications. The second charge related to alleged disparaging
remarks that Accused used to beat his ex-wife. The third charge
alleged that the Accuser suspected that the Accused had sex with
Accuser’s ex-wife.
The Accused in the related Trial Matter No. 2771 was charged
with allegedly making disparaging remarks that he witnessed
Accuser and his ex-wife in a knock-down, drag-out fight.
Despite holding a pre-trial conference, and numerous
communications relating to the time of trial and other pre-trial
requirements, the Accuser failed to timely appear at the time
of trial and arrived 45 minutes after the time scheduled for the
trial and without having returned or communicated with the
Trial Master.
The Trial Master opened the trial. The Accused and his counsel
together with three witnesses for the defense were present. The
Accuser was not present or a counsel was there to represent him.
He was also not available by phone when contacted.
The Accused, through counsel, made a proffer that the three
witnesses named by the Accuser in his charging document will
testify that they did not see or hear anything that would implicate
Accused. In specification number three, Accuser’s ex-wife
submitted a written declaration that she experienced violence at
the hands of the Accuser and denied having sex with the Accused.
With regard to the first charge of unmasonic conduct in matter
No. 2768, the Committee does not believe that the specifications
if true support charges of unmasonic conduct and accordingly
affirm the Trial Master’s decision to dismiss the charge in
that matter.
With regard to the remaining two charges in Matter No. 2768
and Matter No. 2771, based upon a review of the record, the
Trial Review Committee believes that despite the default of the
Accused, the Trial Master should not have accepted the proffer
of by the Accused’s representative and instead conducted an
investigation as contemplated by the California Masonic Code.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

259

Having not performed the investigation contemplated under
the Code, the committee affirms the finding that the Accuser
defaulted and therefore is not remanding the matter for trial, but
recommends that the dismissals of the second and third charge
in Matter No. 2768 and the charges in Matter No. 2771 be reversed
and that the matters be remanded to the Trial Master to perform
the investigation contemplated by the Code.
The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for the
adoption of the following Resolution: “Resolved, that in Trial Numbers
2768 and 2771, the Trial Master’s dismissal be set aside, remand the case
to Trial Master to declare the Accuser in default and thereafter conduct
and investigation only of the Second and Third Charges of Matter No.
2768 and the entire Matter No. 2771.”
Request for Restoration
A request for restoration must address the factors enunciated in
Grand Master Adamson’s Decision No. 3, that is, whether his current
standing, conduct, character, and reputation are such as would make
him worthy of membership in a lodge, the nature of the conduct which
gave rise to his expulsion, the seriousness of the conduct, the passage
of a suitable length of time, the likelihood he will repeat the conduct, his
acceptance of responsibility, remorse and atonement, his efforts to make
amends for the consequences of his conduct, and recommendations of
concerned and knowledgeable Masons and non-Masons.
Case 2580: In 2010, Francisco S. Ibo was expelled by trial from
Masonry for refusal to obey the order of the Grand Master that he
renounce his membership in the Grand and Glorious Order Knights
of the Creeping Serpent, commonly known as the snakes, and that he
provide a list of the members of the organization. In response to the
Grand Master’s order, Mr. Ibo refused to renounce his membership
or provide the list. This year Mr. Ibo again requested restoration by a
letter to Grand Master John R. Heisner stating he was 70-years old and
sought kindness and wisdom. He never submitted any document in
support of his request. This is the third time he has filed an application
for restoration. His two (2) previous applications were denied by the
Grand Lodge. His original application failed to address any of the above
factors under Grand Master Adamson Decision No. 3. In contrast, the
nature of his conduct went well beyond just refusing to obey a directive
of the Grand Master. Mr. Ibo was a member of Benicia Lodge which
has now permanently lost its charter as a result, in part because of his

260

261

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

efforts. Mr. Ibo has not submitted any evidence of his present standing
in the community or that his conduct or character currently are such as
would make him worthy of membership in a lodge. Additionally, he has
submitted no outside verification of his activities in the last seven years
or any information from third parties regarding meritorious conduct.
Based on the inadequacies again in the application, the Committee
recommends a no vote.

Because of the failure of these men to address the factors in 2009
Grand Master Decision No. 3, and because of the lack of any specific
corroborating information, other than generalities attesting to their
good character and rehabilitation, the committee recommends a
no vote.

Cases 2639 and 2640: In 2013, Gary Miranda and Federico Pascua
were expelled from Masonry following trial for striking or hazing a
candidate while he was in the preparation room prior to his third degree.
They previously filed a nearly identical application for restoration last
year that was denied by the Grand Lodge. Mr. Miranda additionally
indicates that he has been volunteering at a local Catholic church
working with children and reading to them. Mr. Miranda and Mr. Pascua
also provided letters coming from Masons, employment, family, and
friends generally confirming how good, helpful, and charitable they are.
However, said letters are all generalities and lacked any specific help,
charity, and good deeds these gentlemen did. In their letters requesting
restoration they generally apologized to the Master and Brethren. It
must be noted that the candidate hazing victim in this case after the
degree executed a handwritten letter detailing the assault or hazing
he suffered at the hands of Mr. Miranda and Mr. Pascua resulting in
the filing of Masonic charges against them. At Miranda and Pascua’s
trial, the victim candidate while under oath was forced to retract the
statements in his handwritten letter to help them in their case. Because
the original letter was corroborated by a witness present when the
hazing occurred, Miranda and Pascua were found guilty. As a result of
the victim candidate’s false testimony, charges for unmasonic conduct
were filed against him. He was found guilty of offering false testimony
and suspended for one year. He accordingly was a victim twice, once for
the hazing and the other for being suspended after trial for one year.
And yet, nowhere in these documents have any proof showing that Mr.
Miranda and Mr. Pascua have apologized to the victim for the physical
assault on his person and for his being placed in a position by them to
offer false testimony to support. Under 2009 Grand Master Decision
Number 3, acceptance of responsibility, remorse and atonement, and
efforts to make amends for the consequences of his conduct must be
shown. This was never addressed nor was any document presented
showing that these gentlemen made amends for their conduct,
particularly to the victim candidate.

The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for the
adoption of the following Resolution: “Resolved, that in Trial Numbers
2580, 2639, and 2640, the applications for restoration be denied.”
Cases 2737 and 2738. The facts of both cases are factually linked as
to nature of the acts constituting the expulsion and to the restoration
petitions. Both Mr. Conrado Montero and Mr. Aldrin Reyes were acting
as Stewards at a degree in 2016 during which the candidate was
assaulted and battered while in the preparation room and, afterwards,
was hoodwinked. No one would take responsibility for the assault
on the candidate. The Trial Master found after a trial that Mr. Reyes,
despite his denials, assaulted the candidate. The Trial Master also
found that Montero lied about Reyes’ presence in the preparation room
during the assault. The Trial Master also found that in addition to his
lying, Montero’s efforts and that of others to deny the assault occurred
caused “mental injury or humiliation” to the candidate. The Trial Master
accordingly ordered that Montero and Reyes be expelled, and Grand
Lodge sustained the penalty.
It has only been one year since Montero and Reyes were expelled,
and in that very short period now seek restoration. The petition and
all supporting documents thereto failed to address the primary basis
set forth for restoration in the 2009 GM Decision No. 3 which, in part,
emphasizes “acceptance of responsibility, remorse, and atonement” for
the conduct giving rise to the expulsion. Both gentlemen failed to accept
any responsibility for their conduct in the letters submitted in support of
restoration. Indeed, they seem to be laboring under the misapprehension
that they were expelled for leaving the room, and because someone
else assaulted the candidate. Neither one of them considers the damage
done to the candidate, to the lodge and to Freemasonry and both claim
a lack of intent calling their acts negligent, which, to the Committee
constitutes a complete denial of that of which they were convicted.
Obviously the lodge has clearly forgiven them as their petitions were
approved by an overwhelming margin, but the unwillingness to accept
responsibility points to an unwillingness to acknowledge the severity
of their conduct and makes them both prime candidates to repeat the

262

263

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

behavior. They need to recognize and acknowledge the damage that
their behavior does to the Fraternity. Moreover, battery is a crime under
section 242 of the California Penal Code, and Grand Lodge should not
forgive a criminal assault on a helpless and blindfolded candidate
so readily. That man has entrusted his well-being to our care and in
this case, during the initiation, we let him down. During the trial the
Accused both emphasized that they were not the regular Stewards and
had no instruction or training. Training is not indispensable, either in
the civil law or in Masonic law, to be able to figure out for yourself
that you do not assault a helpless, blindfolded candidate for any reason.
Until such time that they show remorse, acceptance of responsibility
and rehabilitation, restoration should not be allowed. The Committee
recommends a no vote.

eligibility for membership with respect to conviction of a crime
involving moral turpitude. The provision in point is section 26020
entitled “INELIGIBILITY FOR DEGREES.” It provides that a person
who has pleaded guilty or nolo contendere to, or has been convicted of,
a crime that is morally wrong in itself, is not eligible to apply for the
degrees of Masonry unless, for the reason that he did not commit the
offense, he either has been pardoned or had his judgment of conviction
vacated. This ineligibility for membership due to conviction of a crime
involving moral turpitude was restated in section 804.210 of our present
Code. In addition, section 300.030 of our existing Code provides that
the provisions of this Code, insofar as they are substantially the same
on the date of adoption as then existing statutory provisions relating
to the same subject matter, shall be construed as restatements and
continuations, and not as new enactments. Whether we use the 1991
Code or the 2006 Code, as amended, Mr. Rogacion remains ineligible for
membership due to his conviction of a crime involving moral turpitude.
The votes therefore of his previous lodge and the letters pertaining
to rehabilitation have no relevance with respect to the analysis of his
request for restoration, because until the Code is amended to remove
this ineligibility, he remains disqualified for membership.

The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves
for the adoption of the following Resolution: “Resolved, that in Trial
Numbers 2737 and 2738, the applications for restoration be denied.”
Case 2492. Mr. Pio Rogacion submitted his application to his previous
lodge for the degrees of Masonry on January 31, 1992. In his application,
he answered NO to the question if he has ever been convicted of any
crime. He also answered YES that he carefully reviewed the question
and answered it correctly and truthfully. This was not true because on
June 17, 1983, he was convicted by a San Diego Superior Court under
California Penal Code section 647(a) for child annoyance and required
to register as a sex offender. This conviction is a crime involving moral
turpitude which would have warranted automatic expulsion under
section 1404.820 of the current code. The Code applicable when this
case transpired was our 1991 California Masonic Code. This Code
did not have a mechanism for automatic expulsion. As a result, Mr.
Rogacion was charged for unmasonic conduct for misrepresentation.
The Trial Master found him not guilty. The Committee on Trial Review
recommended reversal of the Trial Master’s findings of not guilty to
guilty and fixed the penalty at expulsion. The Grand Lodge agreed with
our Committee, adjudged Mr. Rogacion guilty for misrepresentation
and imposed the penalty of expulsion.
Mr. Rogacion now comes before this Grand Lodge asking that he
be restored to the rights and privileges of a Master Mason. In support
of his request is a 17-0 vote in favor of restoration from his previous
lodge. He also submitted letters in support of rehabilitation. Let us
revisit the provision of the 1991 California Masonic Code regarding

A part of the records is a June 5, 2005 dismissal order issued by the
San Diego Superior Court granting relief under California Penal Code
Section 1203.4 and 1203.4 A. The dismissal order issued did not mean
he was innocent of the charges. It merely meant that as he has shown
good behavior for a reasonable period of time and the court sealed
or expunged his case. This same document clearly showed that his
conviction remains. The court likewise ordered the Accused to continue
to register as a sex offender. As he committed the offense and this
judgment has never been vacated, the sealing or expungement of his
conviction under California Penal Code Section 1203.4 cannot provide
relief in his request for restoration, the committee recommends a
no vote.
The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for
adoption of the following Resolution: “Resolved, that in Trial Number
2492, the application for restoration be denied.”
Automatic Expulsions
The committee reports that during this Masonic year, in Trial
Numbers 2730, 2791, 2804, 2808, 2809, and 2943, the Grand Master
invoked the automatic expulsion provisions of California Masonic Code

section 1404.820. These cases were based on the accused members’
conviction in federal or state courts of crimes of moral turpitude. The
charges were one for soliciting a minor for lewd or sexual purposes;
one for conspiracy to commit grand theft; one for child molestation; one
for unauthorized access device and credit card fraud; one for voluntary
manslaughter where the victim was stabbed 51 times; and one for
bribery of public officials.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Master, John R. Heisner, and the
members of the Grand Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons of California:
Your Youth Orders Committee proudly continues the long tradition of
service to our youth orders of California and is dedicated to their growth
and success: DeMolay International, Jobs Daughters International, and
the International Order of Rainbow for Girls.
In our second year of the committee restructure and refocus plan,
committeemen were identified and aligned with the Grand Lodge
divisional structure in order to be more effective in working with the
division, district, lodge leadership, and youth orders representatives.
The focus of the committee was also addressed and realigned away
from youth order internal matters and focused on increasing lodge and
member engagement with the orders.
During the year, the Committee embarked on the development
of a long term Strategic Plan focused on a vision of engagement and
involvement. The plan is now drafted and awaits formal adoption by the
Executive Committee of the Grand Lodge before implementation. At the
core of the plan is our vision and mission for the future. The committee
envisions our responsibility as the development of “a Masonic culture
in which the Masons of California, their lodges and the greater Masonic
family are engaged with and are dedicated to the growth and success
of the California Youth Orders.” It defines the committee’s mission as
one in which the committee “considers our Masonic Youth Orders to be
an integral part of the complete Masonic experience and is dedicated
to facilitating the strongest engagement possible among California
Masons, lodges, and the Masonic family with our Masonic Youth Orders.”

266

267

Proceedings of the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

The Strategic Plan identifies four key initiatives/pillars for future
focus and success:

Also in its second year, the committee acted as the facilitator of
raising support for the newly created Arts and Science Educational
Project of the Jobs Daughters. The committee was successful in gaining
commitments for funding to support the educational weekend retreats,
which have already grown to more than 100 youth participants from the
Youth Orders in both Northern and Southern California events.

I.

Establish a culture of Youth Order support by California Masons,
Lodges, and the Grand Lodge of California.

II. Encourage the establishment of a culture of Youth Order
support (sponsorship) by concordant and appendant bodies.
III. Develop and implement a robust communications plan in
cooperation with the Grand Lodge of California to support
Youth Order Committee goals and strategies.
IV. Restructure the Youth Orders Committee, as appropriate, to
effectively execute the plan’s strategies and vision.
Multiple goals and objectives have been identified under each
of the initiatives, which define committee and support activities and
resources. Upon approval, this plan will set the future direction for the
committee and its success.
The committee continued its role as the facilitator of the MAYO
meetings throughout the year. Three MAYO meetings were held: NorCal
DeMolay Convention in November 2016, Grand Assembly in April
2017, and SoCal DeMolay Conclave in September 2017. As part of the
committee’s strategy to expand the involvement with and commitment
to the Youth Orders, leaders from select concordant and appendant
bodies were invited to attend the meetings. I am happy to report that
the leadership from Scottish Rite, Eastern Star, and Amaranth have now
committed to a regular attendance. Leaders from the York Rite bodies
are expected to join us in the upcoming year.
Several situations were brought to the attention of the committee
during the year involving Youth Orders tenancy in Masonic buildings
in which interventions were necessary to help resolve the concerns.
In each case, resolutions were reached although in at least one case
relocation of the Youth Order resulted.
The second year of the newly created LX Youth Leadership
Training was held in conjunction with the Northern California DeMolay
Leadership Camp. Youth leaders from Northern California DeMolay,
Jobs Daughters, and Rainbow Girls participated, and the survey results
were overwhelmingly positive. Commitment to plan for and to conduct
Year 3 has been received.

Grand Master’s Youth Support Awards
The Youth Orders Committee was pleased to forward the names of
the following brothers who were recommended to receive the Grand
Master’s Youth Support Award:
• Brother James A. Jaegar of Naval Lodge No. 87
• Worshipful Brother Isador Ortega of Yosemite Lodge No. 99
• Worshipful Brother Max A. Rush of Montebello-Whittier
Lodge No. 323
• Worshipful Brother John M. Schuster of Palmdale Lodge No. 769
Each was selected by the Grand Master to receive the award in
recognition of his outstanding service to the Masonic Youth Orders and
was honored during the Public Ceremonies on Sunday, October 15, 2017.
The committee would be remiss if it did not recognize and thank the
dedicated leadership of the Youth Orders here in California. Although the
committee realizes that the dedication and service of so many advisors is
necessary, the list would simply be too long for this chronicle. However,
the Executive Officers merit our recognition. A heartfelt thank you
goes out to Terry Peters, Executive Officer for DeMolay International,
Northern California; Dana Regier, Supreme Deputy of California, the
International Order of Rainbow for Girls; Donald Peterson, Executive
Officer for DeMolay International Southern California; Beverly
Graham, Grand Guardian, Jobs Daughters International California; and
Kendall Mills, Associate Grand Guardian, Jobs Daughters International,
California. Thank you for your commitment to our future - our youth.
The members of the committee and I appreciate the confidence and
faith placed in us by Most Worshipful Heisner. It is a great privilege
to serve the craft and continue to support our most precious asset our youth.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
This Committee is honored to have had the opportunity to provide
guidance and direction for California Freemason magazine, the flagship
publication of our Grand Lodge. This year, our Committee was expanded
to bring new, broader viewpoints to the planning process and inform
the magazine’s strategic positioning.
Our priorities this year were to provide in-depth, diverse member
feedback about the magazine and to guide the content strategy – both
editorial and design – for each issue. This year afforded us the unique
opportunity to devote three issues of California Freemason to exploring
the 300th anniversary of organized Freemasonry under the Grand Lodge
of England. The first series of its kind in our magazine, these issues
provided an expansive perspective of the history of the fraternity, its
role today, and how it may evolve in the future.
This commemorative series inspired a special 300th anniversary
collector’s edition of the magazine. The 90-page issue was a bound
compilation of the three issues, with special messages by the Grand
Lodge Executive Committee. A fold out cover provided a poster-like
image of all three magazine covers, which were designed illustrations
inspired by Leonard Gabanon’s iconic illustration “Assemblée des
Francs-Maçons Pour la Réception des Apprentis.” Viewed as a whole,
this artwork depicts the fraternity’s evolution from its past into the
future. The collector’s editions were packaged in a soft-touch handmade
box, embellished with gold foil, along with an exclusively minted
commemorative coin. Each of the 1,000 boxes were hand-numbered.
Our hope is that this commemorative issue will become a treasured
keepsake for California brethren, engendering a sense of pride in
our fraternity.
We are very pleased to report that California Freemason magazine
was commended once again this year by the Folio Awards, a national
organization which for more than 20 years has recognized excellent
publications across a variety of industries – including commercial, nonprofit, and membership organizations. The Folio Awards are highly
regarded in the publishing field and, this year, we are proud to announce
that California Freemason received the following recognitions:

more Masons and community members outside our jurisdiction.
As the reputation of California Freemasonry continues to grow
across the country, we are proud to serve on this committee, and look
forward to being of continued service to our brethren. And, we wish
to thank Vice President of Communications Emily Limón and the
entire Grand Lodge Communications Department for their support
and leadership.

Recognition of Foreign Grand Lodges 2017

(196), Roraima (RR)(196), Santa Catarina (SC)(196), São Paulo (SP)
(198), Sergipe (SE)(203), Tocantins (TO)(204); BULGARIA; United

Burkina Faso*.

The Grand Lodge of California recognizes all of the Grand
Lodges in the United States published in the 2017 List of Lodges
Masonic, which includes all 50 states and the District of Columbia.
In addition, the Grand Lodge of California recognizes a number of
Prince Hall Grand Lodges and foreign Grand Lodges around the
world. The Grand Lodge of California recognizes some, but not all,
of the foreign Grand Lodges in the 2017 List of Lodges Masonic as
well as a number of foreign Grand Lodges that are not listed therein.
For clarity, the foreign Grand Lodges that are recognized by the
Grand Lodge of California are listed below alphabetically by country.
For those that are published in the 2017 List of Lodges Masonic, the
corresponding page number is provided in parenthesis. Recognized
Grand Lodges that are not published in the 2017 List of Lodges
Masonic are marked with an asterisk (*). The Grand Secretary of
the Grand Lodge of California is responsible for all correspondence
with these Grand Lodges and the lodges under their jurisdiction.
Please contact this office for assistance.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

Prince Hall Grand Lodges

The Grand Lodge of California has extended an offer of mutual
recognition with the following Prince Hall Grand Lodges, but mutual
recognition has not yet been established. Visitation between our
members and members of lodges under the jurisdiction of these
Grand Lodges cannot yet be made. When mutual recognition is
established, the Grand Secretary will notify our lodges in writing.

The Grand Lodge of California has mutual recognition with
a number of Prince Hall Grand Lodges in the United States. In
addition, the Grand Lodge of California has extended an offer of
recognition to a number of Prince Hall Grand Lodges throughout
the country where mutual recognition does not yet exist.
The Grand Lodge of California maintains mutual recognition with
following Prince Hall Grand Lodges. Some of these Grand Lodges
are published in the List of Lodges Masonic so the same markings
follow the name of the Grand Lodge to indicate whether or not the
Grand Lodge is published in the List of Lodges Masonic, and if so,
the 2015 edition page number is provided. The terms of recognition
are the same with each Prince Hall Grand Lodge and are consistent
with the agreement of mutual recognition between the Grand Lodge
of California and the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California, Inc.
In essence, dual membership in lodges under the two jurisdictions
is not allowed. Visitation may be had between members of lodges
of both jurisdictions. For these purposes, visitation means visiting
tiled meetings.

To the Board of Trustees
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California
Report on Consolidated Financial Statements
We have audited the accompanying consolidated financial statements of The Most Worshipful Grand
Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California (the “Grand Lodge”), which comprise
the consolidated statement of financial position as of October 31, 2017, and the related consolidated
statements of activities and changes in net assets, and cash flows for the year then ended, and the
related notes to the consolidated financial statements.
Management’s Responsibility for the Consolidated Financial Statements

Management is responsible for the preparation and fair presentation of these consolidated financial
statements in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of
America; this includes the design, implementation, and maintenance of internal control relevant to the
preparation and fair presentation of consolidated financial statements that are free from material
misstatement, whether due to fraud or error.
Auditor’s Responsibility

Our responsibility is to express an opinion on these consolidated financial statements based on our
audit. We conducted our audit in accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in the United
States of America. Those standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable
assurance about whether the consolidated financial statements are free from material misstatement.
An audit involves performing procedures to obtain audit evidence about the amounts and disclosures
in the consolidated financial statements. The procedures selected depend on the auditor’s judgment,
including the assessment of the risks of material misstatement of the consolidated financial statements,
whether due to fraud or error. In making those risk assessments, the auditor considers internal control
relevant to the entity’s preparation and fair presentation of the consolidated financial statements in
order to design audit procedures that are appropriate in the circumstances, but not for the purpose of
expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of the entity’s internal control. Accordingly, we express no
such opinion. An audit also includes evaluating the appropriateness of accounting policies used and
the reasonableness of significant accounting estimates made by management, as well as evaluating
the overall presentation of the consolidated financial statements.
We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis
for our audit opinion.

Opinion

In our opinion, the consolidated financial statements referred to above present fairly, in all material
respects, the financial position of The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of
the State of California as of October 31, 2017, and the changes in its net assets and its cash flows for
the year then ended in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States
of America.
Other Matters – Report on Summarized Comparative Information

We have previously audited the Grand Lodge’s 2016 consolidated financial statements and we
expressed an unmodified opinion on those audited consolidated financial statements in our report dated
April 11, 2017. In our opinion, the summarized comparative information presented herein as of and for
the year ended October 31, 2016, is consistent, in all material respects, with the audited consolidated
financial statements, from which it has been derived.
Other Matter – Supplementary Information

Our audit was conducted for the purpose of forming an opinion on the consolidated financial statements
as a whole. The accompanying consolidating statement of financial position, consolidating statement
of activities and changes in net assets, and consolidating schedule of changes in net assets as of and
for the year ended October 31, 2017, are presented for purposes of additional analysis and are not a
required part of the consolidated financial statements. Such information is the responsibility of
management and was derived from and relates directly to the underlying accounting and other records
used to prepare the consolidated financial statements. Such information has been subjected to the
auditing procedures applied in the audit of the consolidated financial statements and certain additional
procedures, including comparing and reconciling such information directly to the underlying accounting
and other records used to prepare the consolidated financial statements or to the consolidated financial
statements themselves, and other additional procedures in accordance with auditing standards
generally accepted in the United States of America. In our opinion, the information is fairly stated in all
material respects in relation to the consolidated financial statements as a whole.
Other Matter – Other Information

Our audit was conducted for the purpose of forming an opinion on the basic financial statements as a
whole. The accompanying schedule of fraternal expenses, schedule of program appropriations, and
schedule of general and administrative expenses for the years ended October 31, 2017 and 2016, all
presented as supplementary information, are presented for purposes of additional analysis and are not
a required part of the basic consolidated financial statements. Such information has not been subjected
to the auditing procedures applied in the audit of the basic consolidated financial statements, and
accordingly, we do not express an opinion or provide any assurance on it.
